categoryName: Week 6 | Intestinal Disorders, Neoplasia & Anorectal Disease

questions.stem: A neonate born at 28 weeks' gestation weighing 1200 g has been receiving formula feeds in the neonatal intensive care unit. On day of life 10, he develops abdominal distension, feeding intolerance, and several bloody stools. His abdominal wall appears erythematous. An abdominal radiograph demonstrates gas within the bowel wall. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ileocolic intussusception

choices.label: C
choices.text: Necrotizing enterocolitis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mesenteric adenitis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Superior mesenteric artery syndrome

explanation.summary: Necrotizing enterocolitis is the most common gastrointestinal emergency of preterm neonates and is identified by pneumatosis intestinalis on plain radiography.
explanation.whyCorrect: This infant has the classic risk profile for necrotizing enterocolitis: preterm birth at less than 32 weeks with a birth weight under 1500 g and formula feeding. Presentation at 7 to 14 days of life with abdominal distension, feeding intolerance, and bloody stools is typical, and intramural gas (pneumatosis intestinalis) on plain film is the pathognomonic radiographic finding.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pyloric stenosis presents at 3 to 6 weeks with progressive, projectile, nonbilious vomiting and a distended stomach with minimal distal gas, not bloody stools with intramural gas.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Intussusception peaks around 5 to 9 months of age with colicky pain, currant jelly stool, and a target sign on ultrasound; it does not produce gas within the bowel wall.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Correct. Preterm, low-birth-weight, formula-fed infant presenting at day 10 with distension, feeding intolerance, bloody stools, an erythematous abdomen, and pneumatosis intestinalis is necrotizing enterocolitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mesenteric adenitis is a disorder of children with right lower quadrant pain following a viral illness and is not a neonatal disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Superior mesenteric artery syndrome follows rapid weight loss and causes postprandial epigastric pain with bilious vomiting from duodenal compression, not bloody stools or pneumatosis.

questions.stem: A 9-day-old infant born at 27 weeks' gestation develops abdominal distension and feeding intolerance. Necrotizing enterocolitis is suspected, and an abdominal radiograph is obtained. Which of the following radiographic findings would be pathognomonic for this diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Air-fluid levels with stair-stepping of dilated small bowel loops

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gas within the bowel wall

choices.label: C
choices.text: A dilated loop of bowel forming a coffee bean shape

choices.label: D
choices.text: A massively distended stomach with minimal distal gas

choices.label: E
choices.text: Colonic wall thickening with pericolonic fat stranding

explanation.summary: Pneumatosis intestinalis, or intramural gas, is the pathognomonic plain-film finding of necrotizing enterocolitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: In necrotizing enterocolitis, bacterial invasion of the ischemic, immature bowel wall produces gas within the wall itself. Seeing this intramural gas on a plain abdominal radiograph establishes the diagnosis in a preterm neonate with distension and feeding intolerance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dilated loops with air-fluid levels and stair-stepping indicate mechanical small bowel obstruction, a nonspecific pattern that does not establish necrotizing enterocolitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Correct. Intramural gas (pneumatosis intestinalis) is the pathognomonic radiographic finding of necrotizing enterocolitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The coffee bean sign describes sigmoid volvulus, a disease of elderly patients with a redundant sigmoid colon.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A massively distended stomach with minimal distal gas indicates gastric outlet obstruction, such as infantile pyloric stenosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Colonic wall thickening with pericolonic fat stranding is a computed tomography finding of ischemic colitis in older adults.

questions.stem: A neonatology team is designing a protocol to lower the incidence of necrotizing enterocolitis in its very-low-birth-weight infants. Which of the following interventions is the most effective preventive measure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Routine prophylactic systemic antibiotics beginning at birth

choices.label: B
choices.text: Exclusive feeding with cow's-milk formula

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elective placement of a feeding jejunostomy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Daily screening abdominal radiographs

choices.label: E
choices.text: Feeding with maternal breast milk

explanation.summary: Breast milk feeding is the single most effective measure for preventing necrotizing enterocolitis in preterm infants.
explanation.whyCorrect: Breast milk feeding reduces the risk of necrotizing enterocolitis by roughly 50 percent, an effect attributed largely to its influence on the developing intestinal microbiome. Because microbial dysbiosis and formula feeding are central contributors to disease pathogenesis, human milk directly addresses the mechanism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Prophylactic antibiotics are not a preventive strategy; antibiotics are used to treat established disease, and disturbing the microbiome does not lower risk.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Formula feeding is a contributor to the multifactorial pathogenesis of necrotizing enterocolitis rather than a protective measure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A surgical feeding route does not address intestinal immaturity, dysbiosis, or mucosal ischemia and is not a preventive intervention.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Radiographs may detect disease once it develops but do nothing to prevent it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Correct. Maternal breast milk is the most effective preventive measure, reducing risk by about half through effects on the microbiome.

questions.stem: A 12-day-old infant born at 29 weeks' gestation has worsening abdominal distension and bloody stools, and peritonitis is suspected. Which of the following examination findings is most likely to be present in a neonate with peritonitis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A distended, erythematous abdominal wall

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rebound tenderness

choices.label: C
choices.text: Involuntary guarding

choices.label: D
choices.text: Right lower quadrant pain elicited by left lower quadrant palpation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pain on passive extension of the right hip

explanation.summary: Neonates with peritonitis do not display the classic adult peritoneal signs; abdominal wall distension with erythema is the expected finding.
explanation.whyCorrect: Infants lack classic guarding and rebound tenderness even when frank peritonitis is present. Instead, peritoneal inflammation manifests as a distended, erythematous abdomen, which is why abdominal wall discoloration is such an important warning sign in necrotizing enterocolitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Correct. Peritonitis in a neonate is revealed by a distended, erythematous abdomen rather than by classic peritoneal signs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Rebound tenderness is characteristically absent in neonates with peritonitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Involuntary guarding is likewise absent in infants, so its absence cannot be used to exclude peritonitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This describes the Rovsing sign of appendicitis, which is not applicable to a preterm neonate and is not a neonatal peritoneal sign.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pain on passive right hip extension is the psoas sign of a retrocecal appendix, not a finding of neonatal peritonitis.

questions.stem: A 9-day-old infant born at 29 weeks' gestation develops abdominal distension and feeding intolerance. An abdominal radiograph shows gas within the bowel wall with no free intraperitoneal air. He is hemodynamically stable with normal perfusion. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Immediate laparotomy with resection of the involved bowel

choices.label: B
choices.text: Continue current enteral feeds and observe

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pneumatic enema reduction under fluoroscopic guidance

choices.label: D
choices.text: Discontinue enteral feeds and begin antibiotics

choices.label: E
choices.text: Emergent computed tomography angiography of the abdomen

explanation.summary: Mild or early necrotizing enterocolitis without perforation or deterioration is managed medically.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most mild and early cases of necrotizing enterocolitis resolve with medical management alone, consisting of stopping enteral feeds, giving antibiotics, and providing supportive care. Surgery is held in reserve for perforation or clinical deterioration, neither of which is present in this stable infant with no free air.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Operative resection is reserved for perforation or clinical deterioration; this infant is stable with no free air.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Continuing feeds is harmful, since bowel rest is a core element of medical therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Enema reduction is the treatment for pediatric intussusception, not necrotizing enterocolitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Correct. Discontinuing feeds and starting antibiotics with supportive care is the standard medical management, and most early cases resolve with this approach.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Computed tomography angiography is the study of choice for acute mesenteric ischemia in adults, not for a neonate whose diagnosis is already established by plain film.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man with atrial fibrillation who has not been taking his anticoagulant presents with 2 hours of severe, constant periumbilical abdominal pain. He appears distressed, but the abdomen is soft with only mild diffuse tenderness and no rigidity. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ischemic colitis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mesenteric adenitis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Adhesive small bowel obstruction

choices.label: D
choices.text: Acute mesenteric ischemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Intussusception with a tumor lead point

explanation.summary: Pain out of proportion to a benign abdominal examination in a patient with atrial fibrillation is the classic presentation of acute mesenteric ischemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute mesenteric ischemia classically causes severe visceral pain with a soft, relatively benign abdomen early in its course. Atrial fibrillation is the typical source of an arterial embolus, the most acute of the mechanisms producing this syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ischemic colitis presents with abdominal pain followed by hematochezia or bloody diarrhea within 24 hours, which this patient does not have.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mesenteric adenitis is a disease of children and is uncommon after age 20.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Adhesive obstruction produces colicky pain with bilious vomiting, distension, obstipation, and a tympanitic abdomen, not sudden severe pain with a soft abdomen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Correct. Sudden severe pain out of proportion to a soft abdomen in a patient with atrial fibrillation is acute mesenteric ischemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Adult intussusception is uncommon, requires a pathologic lead point, and would present with obstructive symptoms rather than abrupt pain out of proportion to exam.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman presents with the abrupt onset of severe abdominal pain that is markedly out of proportion to a soft abdomen on palpation. Acute mesenteric ischemia is suspected. Which of the following is the diagnostic test of choice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Upright and supine plain abdominal radiographs

choices.label: B
choices.text: Computed tomography angiography of the abdomen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Colonoscopy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serum lactate measurement

choices.label: E
choices.text: Abdominal ultrasound

explanation.summary: Computed tomography angiography is the diagnostic modality of choice for acute mesenteric ischemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Computed tomography angiography directly demonstrates occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery and its branches along with the edematous, ischemic small bowel. It is the test of choice because it identifies both the vascular lesion and the state of the bowel quickly enough to guide operative planning.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Plain films cannot demonstrate mesenteric arterial occlusion and would delay diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Correct. Computed tomography angiography is the diagnostic test of choice and defines the site of occlusion and the extent of bowel involvement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Colonoscopy evaluates the colonic mucosa and is useful in ischemic colitis, not in ischemia of the jejunum and ileum.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Elevated lactate is a late finding, so a lactate level neither establishes nor excludes early ischemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ultrasound is not the modality of choice for evaluating mesenteric arterial occlusion in an adult.

questions.stem: An 83-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation undergoes surgical exploration of the abdomen for peritonitis. At laparotomy, the jejunum and ileum are ischemic while the colon appears normal. Which of the following is the most likely etiology?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cardioembolism to the superior mesenteric artery

choices.label: B
choices.text: Thrombosis of the inferior mesenteric artery

choices.label: C
choices.text: Non-occlusive ischemia caused by vasopressor infusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mesenteric venous thrombosis from an inherited hypercoagulable state

choices.label: E
choices.text: Atheroembolism from the aorta to the celiac artery

explanation.summary: Atrial fibrillation is the classic source of an arterial embolus causing superior mesenteric artery territory ischemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The jejunum and ileum are supplied by the superior mesenteric artery, so ischemia confined to those segments localizes the lesion to that vessel. Arterial embolism is the most acute mechanism of mesenteric ischemia and most often arises from atrial fibrillation, which this patient has.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Correct. An embolus of cardiac origin lodging in the superior mesenteric artery explains ischemia limited to the jejunum and ileum in a patient with atrial fibrillation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the distal colon, so its occlusion would not render the jejunum and ileum ischemic.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Non-occlusive mesenteric ischemia arises in low-flow states such as shock or vasopressor use, neither of which is described here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mesenteric venous thrombosis occurs in hypercoagulable states; no such history is given, and atrial fibrillation points to an arterial embolic source.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The celiac artery supplies foregut structures; its occlusion would not produce isolated jejunal and ileal ischemia.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man is in the intensive care unit with septic shock requiring high-dose vasopressor infusions. On hospital day 3 he develops abdominal distension and pain, and imaging shows edematous small bowel without occlusion of the major mesenteric vessels. Which of the following mechanisms best explains his intestinal ischemia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Embolus from the left atrium lodging in the superior mesenteric artery

choices.label: B
choices.text: Thrombosis of the superior mesenteric vein

choices.label: C
choices.text: Acute thrombosis of a chronically atherosclerotic superior mesenteric artery

choices.label: D
choices.text: Telescoping of one bowel segment into another

choices.label: E
choices.text: Non-occlusive ischemia from a low-flow state

explanation.summary: Non-occlusive mesenteric ischemia results from low-flow states such as shock or vasopressor use, with patent major vessels.
explanation.whyCorrect: This patient is in shock and receiving vasopressors, the classic setting for non-occlusive mesenteric ischemia. The absence of occlusion in the major mesenteric vessels despite ischemic-appearing bowel confirms that hypoperfusion, not a mechanical occlusion, is responsible.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An embolic mechanism would show occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery, and no cardiac embolic source such as atrial fibrillation is described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mesenteric venous thrombosis arises from hypercoagulable states and would demonstrate venous thrombus on imaging.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Arterial thrombosis occurs on a background of chronic atherosclerotic disease of the superior mesenteric artery and would produce arterial occlusion on imaging.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intussusception is a mechanical telescoping of bowel and is not caused by shock or vasopressors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Correct. Shock and vasopressor-induced vasoconstriction produce non-occlusive mesenteric ischemia with patent major vessels.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with a known inherited thrombophilia and a prior unprovoked deep venous thrombosis presents with several days of worsening abdominal pain. She is in sinus rhythm and normotensive, and imaging demonstrates thrombus within the mesenteric vein with edematous small bowel loops. Which of the following mechanisms of acute mesenteric ischemia is present?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Arterial embolism from atrial fibrillation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Non-occlusive ischemia from shock or vasopressors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mesenteric venous thrombosis related to a hypercoagulable state

choices.label: D
choices.text: Arterial thrombosis of an atherosclerotic superior mesenteric artery

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transient hypoperfusion of a colonic watershed area

explanation.summary: Mesenteric venous thrombosis is the mechanism of acute mesenteric ischemia associated with hypercoagulable states.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute mesenteric ischemia has four mechanisms, and venous thrombosis is the one driven by hypercoagulability. This young patient has an inherited thrombophilia and prior venous thrombosis, and imaging directly demonstrates venous thrombus with congested, edematous bowel.

whyWrongByChoice.A: She is in sinus rhythm with no cardiac embolic source, and imaging shows venous rather than arterial occlusion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Non-occlusive ischemia requires a low-flow state such as shock or vasopressor therapy; she is normotensive.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Correct. Thrombus in the mesenteric vein in a patient with an inherited thrombophilia is mesenteric venous thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Arterial thrombosis develops on chronic atherosclerotic disease of the superior mesenteric artery, which is not expected in a 34-year-old with a thrombophilia and venous thrombus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Watershed hypoperfusion describes ischemic colitis of the splenic flexure or rectosigmoid, not thrombosis of a mesenteric vein with small bowel edema.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man presents 2 hours after the sudden onset of excruciating abdominal pain. He is writhing in discomfort, yet the abdomen is soft with minimal tenderness and no rigidity. Which of the following best explains the discrepancy between his severe pain and his benign abdominal examination?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The ischemic bowel has already infarcted and become insensate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Visceral pain from hypoperfusion precedes peritoneal involvement

choices.label: C
choices.text: Serum lactate has not yet risen high enough to sensitize the abdominal wall

choices.label: D
choices.text: Collateral circulation has fully compensated, so the bowel is not ischemic

choices.label: E
choices.text: Gas and fluid have not yet accumulated proximal to a mechanical obstruction

explanation.summary: Early mesenteric ischemia produces severe visceral pain with a benign exam because the parietal peritoneum is not yet inflamed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hypoperfused bowel generates intense visceral pain, but peritoneal signs require inflammation to reach the parietal peritoneum. Until ischemia becomes transmural, the abdomen remains soft, producing the classic pain out of proportion to examination.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The pain is severe rather than absent, and infarcted transmural bowel produces peritonitis rather than a benign abdomen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Correct. Visceral pain from hypoperfusion precedes transmural necrosis and involvement of the parietal peritoneum, so the exam remains benign early.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lactate elevation is a late marker of ischemia and does not determine the presence of peritoneal signs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Adequate collateral flow would relieve the ischemia and the pain, which is not the case here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This describes the pathophysiology of mechanical bowel obstruction, which causes colicky pain with distension rather than sudden severe pain with a soft abdomen.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man is diagnosed with acute mesenteric ischemia. Which of the following bowel segments is most likely to be involved?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Splenic flexure and rectosigmoid junction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cecum and ascending colon

choices.label: C
choices.text: Stomach and proximal duodenum

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sigmoid colon alone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Jejunum and ileum

explanation.summary: Acute mesenteric ischemia predominantly involves the superior mesenteric artery territory, which is the jejunum and ileum.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute mesenteric ischemia primarily affects the distribution of the superior mesenteric artery, namely the jejunum and ileum. This territorial distinction is what separates it from ischemic colitis, which involves colonic segments.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The splenic flexure and rectosigmoid junction are the colonic watershed areas affected in ischemic colitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The cecum and right colon are the usual sites of angiodysplasia and are not the characteristic territory of acute mesenteric ischemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The stomach and proximal duodenum are foregut structures and are not in the superior mesenteric artery ischemic territory described here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Isolated sigmoid involvement suggests a colonic process such as diverticular disease or volvulus rather than acute mesenteric ischemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Correct. Acute mesenteric ischemia primarily affects the superior mesenteric artery territory of the jejunum and ileum.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation has computed tomography angiography demonstrating occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery with severely edematous small bowel. She is taken to the operating room, where a segment of jejunum and ileum is frankly necrotic. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics alone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endoscopic decompression of the involved bowel segment

choices.label: C
choices.text: Embolectomy followed by resection of necrotic bowel

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hydrostatic saline enema reduction under ultrasound guidance

choices.label: E
choices.text: Bowel rest with nasogastric decompression and observation

explanation.summary: Treatment of embolic acute mesenteric ischemia is revascularization plus resection of nonviable bowel.
explanation.whyCorrect: Surgical embolectomy or thrombectomy restores perfusion to the remaining bowel, and any segment that is already necrotic must be resected. Both steps are required, since revascularization alone leaves dead bowel behind and resection alone leaves the remaining intestine hypoperfused.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibiotics do not restore mesenteric blood flow or remove necrotic bowel, and necrotic intestine will progress to sepsis and death.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Endoscopic decompression is the initial treatment of sigmoid volvulus, not of arterial occlusion with necrotic small bowel.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Correct. Embolectomy restores flow and necrotic segments are resected, which is the definitive operative management.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Enema reduction is used for pediatric intussusception and has no role in mesenteric arterial occlusion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nonoperative management is appropriate for uncomplicated adhesive small bowel obstruction, not for necrotic bowel from arterial occlusion.

questions.stem: A 7-month-old previously healthy boy is brought in with recurrent episodes of inconsolable crying during which he draws his legs toward his abdomen, separated by intervals in which he appears comfortable. He has had one stool mixed with blood and mucus. A sausage-shaped mass is palpable in the right side of the abdomen. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Intussusception

choices.label: B
choices.text: Necrotizing enterocolitis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mesenteric adenitis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Acute appendicitis

explanation.summary: Colicky pain, currant jelly stool, and a palpable sausage-shaped mass form the classic triad of pediatric intussusception.
explanation.whyCorrect: Intussusception peaks between 5 and 9 months of age and is usually ileocolic and idiopathic, with lymphoid hyperplasia serving as the lead point. This infant demonstrates all three elements of the classic triad, which are often incomplete but here are fully present.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Correct. Episodic colicky pain, blood and mucus in the stool, and a sausage-shaped abdominal mass in an infant of this age indicate intussusception.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Necrotizing enterocolitis affects preterm neonates in the first weeks of life, not a healthy 7-month-old.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pyloric stenosis presents at 3 to 6 weeks with progressive projectile nonbilious vomiting, without bloody stool or an abdominal mass.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mesenteric adenitis causes right lower quadrant pain and fever after a viral illness in older children, without a sausage-shaped mass or currant jelly stool.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Appendicitis peaks in the second and third decades and would cause pain migrating to the right lower quadrant with localized tenderness rather than episodic colic with a palpable mass.

questions.stem: An 8-month-old girl has intermittent episodes of severe crampy abdominal pain alternating with lethargy, and bilious vomiting has begun. Abdominal ultrasound is performed. Which of the following findings would confirm the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gas within the wall of the small bowel

choices.label: B
choices.text: A thickened pyloric muscle

choices.label: C
choices.text: Clustered enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes with a normal appendix

choices.label: D
choices.text: Concentric rings producing a target appearance

choices.label: E
choices.text: Colonic wall thickening with surrounding fat stranding

explanation.summary: The target, or donut, sign on ultrasound confirms intussusception.
explanation.whyCorrect: Telescoping of one bowel segment into another produces concentric layers of bowel wall that appear as rings on cross-sectional ultrasound, the target or donut sign. This infant's episodic colic with lethargy and bilious vomiting from small bowel obstruction fits intussusception, and the target sign confirms it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Intramural gas is the pathognomonic finding of necrotizing enterocolitis, a disease of preterm neonates.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A thickened pyloric muscle confirms pyloric stenosis, which presents at 3 to 6 weeks with nonbilious vomiting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Enlarged mesenteric nodes with a normal appendix indicate mesenteric adenitis, which does not cause episodic colic with bilious vomiting in an 8-month-old.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Correct. The target (donut) sign of concentric rings is the sonographic finding of intussusception.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Colonic wall thickening with pericolonic fat stranding describes ischemic colitis in elderly patients.

questions.stem: A 9-month-old boy has ultrasound-confirmed ileocolic intussusception. He is well perfused and hemodynamically stable, the abdomen is soft without peritoneal signs, and there is no evidence of perforation. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Immediate laparoscopic resection of the involved bowel

choices.label: B
choices.text: Observation with serial abdominal examinations alone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pneumatic enema reduction under fluoroscopic guidance

choices.label: D
choices.text: Colonoscopic decompression

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nasogastric decompression as definitive therapy

explanation.summary: Pneumatic or hydrostatic enema reduction is the first-line treatment of intussusception in children.
explanation.whyCorrect: In children, intussusception is reduced nonoperatively with air or saline instilled under fluoroscopic or ultrasound guidance. Surgery is reserved for failed reduction, perforation, or a suspected pathologic lead point, none of which is present in this stable infant.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Operative management is reserved for failed enema reduction, perforation, or a suspected pathologic lead point.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Observation alone leaves the obstruction unreduced and risks progression to ischemia and perforation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Correct. Pneumatic (air) enema reduction under fluoroscopic guidance is the first-line therapy for pediatric intussusception.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Colonoscopic decompression is the initial treatment of sigmoid volvulus, not of pediatric intussusception.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nasogastric decompression is supportive and does not reduce the telescoped bowel.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with several weeks of intermittent crampy abdominal pain undergoes computed tomography, which demonstrates a segment of small bowel telescoped into the adjacent segment. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lymphoid hyperplasia acting as a lead point

choices.label: B
choices.text: A polyp or tumor acting as a pathologic lead point

choices.label: C
choices.text: A preceding Yersinia enterocolitica enteritis infection

choices.label: D
choices.text: Postoperative adhesive bands from a prior laparotomy

choices.label: E
choices.text: An inherited hypercoagulable state such as factor V Leiden

explanation.summary: Intussusception in adults is uncommon and is usually driven by a pathologic lead point such as a polyp or tumor.
explanation.whyCorrect: A lead point is a mass pulled forward by peristalsis, dragging one bowel segment into another. Unlike the idiopathic, lymphoid-hyperplasia-related disease of infants, adult intussusception is rare and typically signals an underlying polyp or tumor that must be identified.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lymphoid hyperplasia is the usual lead point in young children, in whom the disease is considered idiopathic.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Correct. Adult intussusception is uncommon and usually caused by a pathologic lead point such as a polyp or tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Yersinia enterocolitica is a classic trigger of mesenteric adenitis, not of adult intussusception.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Adhesions are the leading cause of mechanical small bowel obstruction but do not create the intraluminal lead point that produces telescoping.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hypercoagulability leads to mesenteric venous thrombosis, not to intussusception.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy has 2 days of right lower quadrant pain, low-grade fever, and vomiting following an upper respiratory infection the week before. Tenderness is diffuse and shifts location when he changes position, and there are no peritoneal signs. Leukocyte count is 8,200/mm3 with a relative lymphocytosis. Ultrasound shows clustered enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes and a normal-appearing appendix. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute appendicitis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intussusception

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ischemic colitis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Necrotizing enterocolitis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mesenteric adenitis

explanation.summary: Mesenteric adenitis mimics appendicitis but shows enlarged mesenteric nodes with a normal appendix and a lymphocyte-predominant count.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mesenteric adenitis is inflammation of mesenteric lymph nodes, commonly triggered by a preceding viral illness such as an upper respiratory infection. Tenderness that is less localized and shifts with repositioning, absent peritoneal signs, a lower white count with relative lymphocytosis, and enlarged nodes with a normal appendix on imaging all point to this diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Appendicitis would show a dilated, inflamed appendix on imaging and typically a mild leukocytosis with a left shift, not a normal appendix with lymphocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Intussusception peaks in infancy, presents with episodic colic and currant jelly stool, and would show a target sign rather than clustered lymph nodes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ischemic colitis affects elderly patients and causes pain followed by hematochezia with colonic wall thickening.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Necrotizing enterocolitis occurs in preterm neonates, not in school-age children.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Correct. Enlarged mesenteric nodes with a normal appendix after a viral upper respiratory infection, with shifting tenderness and relative lymphocytosis, is mesenteric adenitis.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl with right lower quadrant pain and fever is found on computed tomography to have clustered right lower quadrant lymph nodes measuring 7 mm with a normal appendix and no periappendiceal inflammation. She is well hydrated and comfortable after analgesia. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Intravenous fluids and analgesia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Laparoscopic appendectomy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pneumatic enema reduction under fluoroscopy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Segmental resection of the involved small bowel

choices.label: E
choices.text: Long-term systemic anticoagulation with warfarin

explanation.summary: Mesenteric adenitis is self-limited and is treated supportively, and recognizing it prevents an unnecessary operation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Enlarged clustered right lower quadrant nodes of 5 mm or more with a normal appendix establish mesenteric adenitis. The illness resolves on its own within 1 to 4 weeks without specific treatment, so management is limited to hydration and analgesics, and correct recognition avoids unnecessary surgery.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Correct. Mesenteric adenitis is self-limited over 1 to 4 weeks and requires only hydration and analgesia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The appendix is normal on imaging, so appendectomy would be exactly the unnecessary operation that recognizing this diagnosis is meant to prevent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Enema reduction treats intussusception, which is not suggested by clustered lymph nodes and a normal appendix.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bowel resection is used for necrotic or nonviable intestine and has no role in inflamed mesenteric lymph nodes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anticoagulation addresses thrombotic vascular disease such as mesenteric venous thrombosis, not lymph node inflammation.

questions.stem: A neonate born at 27 weeks' gestation develops advanced necrotizing enterocolitis with perforation and undergoes laparotomy, at which a large length of necrotic jejunum and ileum is resected. Which of the following long-term complications is she at greatest risk of developing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mesenteric adenitis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ischemic colitis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Short bowel syndrome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Colonic diverticulosis

explanation.summary: Extensive intestinal resection, as required in severe necrotizing enterocolitis, leads to short bowel syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Severe necrotizing enterocolitis can produce necrotic bowel that must be surgically resected, and extensive intestinal loss results in short bowel syndrome. The greater the length of jejunum and ileum removed, the greater the risk.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pyloric stenosis is congenital hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle presenting at 3 to 6 weeks and is unrelated to small bowel resection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mesenteric adenitis is a self-limited inflammation of mesenteric lymph nodes in older children triggered by infection, not a consequence of resection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ischemic colitis results from transient hypoperfusion of colonic watershed areas and predominantly affects the elderly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Correct. Extensive loss of small intestine after resection for severe necrotizing enterocolitis causes short bowel syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Diverticulosis is an acquired colonic condition that becomes common with advancing age.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of abdominal pain that began 18 hours ago around the umbilicus and has since settled into the right lower quadrant. He has had no appetite since the pain began and vomited once. His temperature is 37.9 C (100.2 F). Examination shows maximal tenderness two-thirds of the way along a line from the umbilicus to the right anterior superior iliac spine, with voluntary guarding. Leukocyte count is 13,500/mm3 with a left shift. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mesenteric adenitis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acute diverticulitis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ischemic colitis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Acute appendicitis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ileocolic intussusception

explanation.summary: This item tests recognition of the classic presentation of acute appendicitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute appendicitis classically begins as periumbilical visceral pain that migrates to the right lower quadrant within 24 hours as inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum overlying McBurney's point. Anorexia is present in about 85% of patients and typically follows the onset of pain, and mild leukocytosis with a left shift is expected. Peak incidence is in the second and third decades, matching this patient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mesenteric adenitis produces less localized tenderness that shifts with repositioning, fewer peritoneal signs, and a lower leukocyte count with relative lymphocytosis rather than neutrophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Diverticulitis in Western populations is predominantly sigmoid and presents with left lower quadrant pain and tenderness, usually in older patients.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ischemic colitis predominantly affects the elderly and presents with abdominal pain followed by hematochezia or bloody diarrhea within 24 hours.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Correct: periumbilical pain migrating to McBurney's point with anorexia after pain onset and mild leukocytosis with left shift is the classic appendicitis picture.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Intussusception peaks at 5 to 9 months of age with colicky pain, currant jelly stool, and a sausage-shaped mass; in adults it is uncommon and requires a pathologic lead point.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy undergoes laparoscopic appendectomy for acute appendicitis. Which of the following most likely initiated the disease process in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Atherosclerotic occlusion of the appendiceal artery

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lymphoid hyperplasia obstructing the appendiceal lumen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Telescoping of the terminal ileum into the cecum

choices.label: D
choices.text: Herniation of mucosa and submucosa through the muscular wall

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transient hypoperfusion of a colonic watershed segment

explanation.summary: This item tests the initiating event in appendicitis and how its cause varies with age.
explanation.whyCorrect: Appendicitis begins with luminal obstruction, which in younger patients is most often caused by lymphoid hyperplasia. Appendicoliths are the more common obstructing cause in older patients, and tumors may also obstruct the lumen in adults. Obstruction raises intraluminal pressure, leading to ischemia and bacterial invasion of the wall.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Large-vessel atherosclerotic occlusion describes the mechanism of arterial thrombotic mesenteric ischemia, not the initiating event in appendicitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Correct: lymphoid hyperplasia is the most common cause of appendiceal luminal obstruction in younger patients.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Telescoping of bowel describes intussusception, a separate entity that peaks in infancy and typically involves the ileocolic region.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Herniation of mucosa and submucosa through the muscular layer at sites of vasa recta penetration describes colonic pseudodiverticula.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transient hypoperfusion of watershed segments describes ischemic colitis, which affects the splenic flexure and rectosigmoid junction in the elderly.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman develops vague, poorly localized periumbilical abdominal pain. Several hours later the pain becomes sharp and localized to the right lower quadrant, and CT of the abdomen shows a 9-mm tubular structure in the right lower quadrant with surrounding inflammation. The early periumbilical pain is referred to a dermatome supplied by which of the following spinal levels?

choices.label: A
choices.text: T4

choices.label: B
choices.text: T8

choices.label: E
choices.text: L2

explanation.summary: This item tests the neuroanatomic basis of early periumbilical pain in appendicitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The distended appendix stimulates visceral afferent fibers traveling with sympathetic fibers from T8 through T10. Midgut visceral pain is referred to the periumbilical region because these visceral pain fibers enter the spinal cord at T10, which corresponds to the umbilical dermatome. Localization to the right lower quadrant occurs later, when inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum.

whyWrongByChoice.A: T4 corresponds to the nipple line and is far above the level to which midgut visceral pain is referred.
whyWrongByChoice.B: T8 is within the range of sympathetic fibers carrying appendiceal afferents, but the dermatome to which the pain is referred is the umbilical level.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Correct: T10 is the umbilical dermatome, and midgut visceral afferents entering the cord at T10 produce periumbilical pain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: T12 lies below the umbilicus and does not account for periumbilical referral of midgut visceral pain.
whyWrongByChoice.E: L2 is well below the umbilical dermatome and does not receive the midgut visceral afferents responsible for this pain.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man has had right lower quadrant abdominal pain for one day. On examination, passive extension of the right hip while he lies on his left side reproduces right lower quadrant pain. This finding most strongly suggests which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A retrocecal position of the inflamed appendix

choices.label: B
choices.text: A pelvic position of the inflamed appendix

choices.label: C
choices.text: Perforation with generalized peritonitis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes with a normal appendix

choices.label: E
choices.text: An obstructing appendicolith at the appendiceal base

explanation.summary: This item tests the anatomic significance of the psoas sign.
explanation.whyCorrect: The psoas sign is right lower quadrant pain elicited by passive extension of the right hip. It suggests an inflamed retrocecal appendix lying against the psoas muscle, so that stretching the muscle irritates the adjacent inflamed organ.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Correct: a positive psoas sign points to a retrocecal appendix.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A pelvic appendix is suggested by the obturator sign, which is elicited by internal rotation of the flexed right hip.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Generalized peritonitis from perforation produces diffuse rigidity and tenderness rather than a position-dependent maneuver sign.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mesenteric adenitis characteristically produces less localized tenderness and fewer peritoneal signs, not a positional sign referable to the psoas muscle.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An appendicolith is an obstructing cause identified on imaging and cannot be inferred from a hip extension maneuver.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with suspected acute appendicitis is examined. With the right hip and knee flexed, internal rotation of the right hip reproduces right lower quadrant pain. This finding most strongly suggests which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A retrocecal position of the inflamed appendix

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inflammation of mesenteric lymph nodes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Generalized peritonitis from perforation

choices.label: D
choices.text: A periappendiceal abscess walled off by omentum

choices.label: E
choices.text: A pelvic position of the inflamed appendix

explanation.summary: This item tests the anatomic significance of the obturator sign.
explanation.whyCorrect: The obturator sign is right lower quadrant pain produced by internal rotation of the flexed right hip. It suggests an inflamed appendix lying in the pelvis, adjacent to the obturator internus muscle.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A retrocecal appendix is suggested by the psoas sign, elicited by passive extension of the right hip.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mesenteric adenitis produces less localized tenderness that may shift with repositioning, and peritoneal signs are less common.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Generalized peritonitis causes diffuse tenderness and rigidity rather than a maneuver-specific localized pain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A walled-off abscess is a complication defined by imaging findings and is not diagnosed by hip rotation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Correct: a positive obturator sign points to a pelvic appendix.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man is evaluated for right lower quadrant pain. The examining physician wishes to elicit the Rovsing sign. Which of the following maneuvers should be performed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Passive extension of the right hip

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deep palpation of the left lower quadrant

choices.label: C
choices.text: Internal rotation of the flexed right hip

choices.label: D
choices.text: Palpation two-thirds of the way from the umbilicus to the anterior superior iliac spine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Percussion of the abdomen to assess for tympany

explanation.summary: This item tests how the Rovsing sign is elicited.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Rovsing sign is right lower quadrant pain produced by palpation of the left lower quadrant. It has good specificity for appendicitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Passive right hip extension elicits the psoas sign, which suggests a retrocecal appendix.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Correct: palpating the left lower quadrant and eliciting pain in the right lower quadrant defines the Rovsing sign.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Internal rotation of the flexed right hip elicits the obturator sign, which suggests a pelvic appendix.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Palpation at that location tests for the McBurney sign, the most sensitive and specific sign of appendicitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Percussion for tympany assesses abdominal distension, as in bowel obstruction, and is not the Rovsing maneuver.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old girl is evaluated for suspected acute appendicitis. The physician documents tenderness at McBurney's point. This point is located at which of the following sites?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The midpoint of a line from the umbilicus to the pubic symphysis

choices.label: B
choices.text: One-third of the way from the umbilicus to the right anterior superior iliac spine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two-thirds of the way from the umbilicus to the right anterior superior iliac spine

choices.label: D
choices.text: At the right costal margin in the midclavicular line

choices.label: E
choices.text: The midpoint of a line from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle

explanation.summary: This item tests the surface anatomy of McBurney's point.
explanation.whyCorrect: McBurney's point lies two-thirds of the distance from the umbilicus to the anterior superior iliac spine. Tenderness there reflects inflammation of the overlying parietal peritoneum and is the most sensitive and specific examination sign of appendicitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This midline suprapubic location does not correspond to the parietal peritoneum overlying the appendix.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The point lies two-thirds, not one-third, of the way toward the anterior superior iliac spine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Correct: McBurney's point is two-thirds of the way from the umbilicus to the anterior superior iliac spine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The right costal margin overlies the hepatobiliary region rather than the appendix.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This inguinal landmark is not the location where appendiceal parietal peritoneal inflammation is detected.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of right lower quadrant abdominal pain and vomiting for one day. Her temperature is 38.1 C (100.6 F) and she has right lower quadrant tenderness. Appendicitis is suspected, and the physician wants to minimize radiation exposure. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial imaging study?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ultrasonography of the right lower quadrant

choices.label: B
choices.text: CT of the abdomen with intravenous contrast

choices.label: C
choices.text: Supine and upright plain abdominal radiographs

choices.label: D
choices.text: CT angiography of the abdomen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Colonoscopy

explanation.summary: This item tests imaging selection for suspected appendicitis in children.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ultrasonography is preferred in children and pregnant patients because it avoids ionizing radiation. It can show an enlarged appendix in short and long axis, a thickened appendiceal wall, and an appendicolith with acoustic shadowing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Correct: ultrasonography is the preferred initial study in children in order to avoid radiation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CT is the imaging procedure of choice in general practice but delivers ionizing radiation, which is what this physician is trying to avoid in a child.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Plain radiographs are used to evaluate bowel obstruction patterns and do not establish appendicitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CT angiography is the test of choice for acute mesenteric ischemia, not appendicitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Colonoscopy is used to assess colonic mucosa and the level of colonic obstruction, not acute appendicitis.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man has had right lower quadrant abdominal pain for 12 hours. His temperature is 37.6 C (99.7 F), leukocyte count is 11,200/mm3, and abdominal examination is equivocal, with mild tenderness but no guarding. Which of the following is the most appropriate imaging study to confirm the diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ultrasonography of the right lower quadrant

choices.label: B
choices.text: Supine and upright plain abdominal radiographs

choices.label: C
choices.text: Barium enema

choices.label: D
choices.text: CT angiography of the abdomen

choices.label: E
choices.text: CT of the abdomen

explanation.summary: This item tests the imaging modality of choice for suspected appendicitis in adults.
explanation.whyCorrect: CT of the abdomen is the imaging procedure of choice for appendicitis. It demonstrates appendiceal dilation and fluid greater than 6 mm, periappendiceal inflammation, and an appendicolith, and its widespread use has reduced the negative appendectomy rate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ultrasonography is reserved preferentially for children and pregnant patients to avoid radiation, not for a nonpregnant adult man.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Plain radiographs are useful for identifying bowel obstruction and do not diagnose appendicitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Barium enema does not evaluate the appendiceal wall or periappendiceal inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CT angiography is the diagnostic test of choice for acute mesenteric ischemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Correct: CT of the abdomen is the imaging procedure of choice for suspected appendicitis.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman has had periumbilical pain that migrated to the right lower quadrant over 20 hours, with anorexia and nausea. CT of the abdomen is performed. Which of the following findings would most strongly support the diagnosis of acute appendicitis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Diffuse colonic wall thickening with pericolonic fat stranding centered at the splenic flexure

choices.label: B
choices.text: A dilated 9-mm blind-ending tubular structure in the right lower quadrant

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gas within the bowel wall

choices.label: D
choices.text: Concentric rings of bowel within bowel in the right abdomen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dilated proximal small bowel loops with a transition point and collapsed distal bowel

explanation.summary: This item tests the CT findings of acute appendicitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: CT findings of appendicitis include appendiceal dilation with fluid greater than 6 mm in diameter, periappendiceal inflammation, and an appendicolith. A 9-mm right lower quadrant tubular structure with surrounding fat stranding satisfies these criteria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Colonic wall thickening with pericolonic fat stranding at a watershed area is the CT appearance of ischemic colitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Correct: an appendix greater than 6 mm with periappendiceal inflammation is the characteristic CT finding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Intramural gas is pneumatosis intestinalis, the pathognomonic radiographic finding of necrotizing enterocolitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bowel-within-bowel concentric rings represent the target or donut appearance of intussusception.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dilated small bowel with a transition point and collapsed distal bowel indicates small bowel obstruction.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man is diagnosed with uncomplicated acute appendicitis, without perforation, abscess, or phlegmon. Which of the following is the definitive treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Endoscopic decompression

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hydrostatic enema reduction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Laparoscopic appendectomy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nasogastric decompression, bowel rest, and intravenous fluids

choices.label: E
choices.text: Elective sigmoid colectomy

explanation.summary: This item tests definitive management of acute appendicitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Laparoscopic appendectomy is the definitive treatment of acute appendicitis. Compared with open surgery, it offers faster recovery and a lower rate of surgical site infection. Preoperative antibiotics covering gram-negative rods and anaerobes are given as standard.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Endoscopic decompression is the initial treatment of sigmoid volvulus, not appendicitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pneumatic or hydrostatic enema reduction is the treatment for pediatric intussusception.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Correct: laparoscopic appendectomy is the definitive treatment and has faster recovery and fewer surgical site infections than open appendectomy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bowel rest, nasogastric decompression, and fluids constitute the initial nonoperative management of adhesive small bowel obstruction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Elective sigmoid colectomy is offered for recurrent diverticulitis based on episode frequency, severity, and quality-of-life impact.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman is scheduled for laparoscopic appendectomy for acute appendicitis. Preoperative antibiotics are administered. This regimen is selected principally to provide coverage against which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Candida albicans

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gram-negative rods and anaerobes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vancomycin-resistant enterococci

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mycobacterial species

explanation.summary: This item tests the antimicrobial spectrum required for appendectomy prophylaxis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Preoperative antibiotics for appendectomy must cover gram-negative rods and anaerobes, the enteric flora released from an inflamed appendix. Standard options include a single dose of cefoxitin or cefotetan, or cefazolin plus metronidazole.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Resistant staphylococci are not the target flora of appendiceal infection, and the standard cephalosporin-based regimens do not cover them.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fungal coverage is not part of standard prophylaxis for appendectomy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Correct: the standard regimens are chosen to cover gram-negative rods and anaerobes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Resistant enterococcal coverage is not the goal of the cephalosporin or cephalosporin-plus-metronidazole regimens used here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mycobacteria play no role in acute appendicitis and are not targeted by preoperative prophylaxis.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man undergoes laparoscopic appendectomy after 3 days of right lower quadrant pain. At operation the appendix is gangrenous and perforated, with purulent fluid in the pelvis. Compared with a patient whose appendix was not perforated, this patient is at greatest risk for which of the following postoperative complications?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Intra-abdominal abscess

choices.label: B
choices.text: Recurrent diverticular bleeding

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sigmoid volvulus with colonic ischemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Short bowel syndrome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pneumobilia

explanation.summary: This item tests the principal postoperative complication of perforated appendicitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Perforation releases bacteria and pus into the peritoneal cavity, which increases the risk of postoperative abscess. For this reason, postoperative antibiotics are continued when perforation has occurred, whereas they are unnecessary after appendectomy for nonperforated disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Correct: perforation increases the risk of postoperative intra-abdominal abscess.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Diverticular bleeding results from arterial rupture at the neck of a colonic diverticulum and is unrelated to appendectomy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sigmoid volvulus is associated with elderly, institutionalized patients with chronic constipation and a redundant sigmoid colon.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Short bowel syndrome follows extensive small bowel resection, as in advanced necrotizing enterocolitis or mesenteric ischemia, not appendectomy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pneumobilia indicates a communication between the biliary tree and the gut, as in gallstone ileus with a cholecystoenteric fistula.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man has had progressively worsening right lower quadrant abdominal pain for 3 days but has avoided seeking care. If his untreated appendicitis continues to progress, which of the following outcomes is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic appendiceal stricture causing colonic obstruction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fistula between the gallbladder and duodenum

choices.label: C
choices.text: Telescoping of the appendix into the cecum

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gangrene and perforation with abscess formation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spontaneous resolution with diverticular outpouching

explanation.summary: This item tests the natural history of untreated appendicitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: If untreated, appendicitis progresses from ischemia and bacterial invasion of the wall to gangrene and perforation. Perforation results in either a localized abscess contained by the omentum or generalized peritonitis. Symptoms lasting longer than 24 hours increase perforation risk, although perforation can occur earlier.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chronic fibrotic stricture causing large bowel narrowing is a feature of recurrent diverticulitis of the sigmoid colon.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A cholecystoenteric fistula is the mechanism of gallstone ileus and is unrelated to appendiceal inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Telescoping describes intussusception, which requires a lead point and is not the natural course of appendicitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Correct: untreated appendicitis progresses to gangrene and perforation with abscess or generalized peritonitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Colonic diverticula are pseudodiverticula that form at sites of vasa recta penetration and are not an outcome of appendicitis.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man is evaluated for 16 hours of right lower quadrant pain with anorexia and tenderness at McBurney's point. Which of the following laboratory findings is most likely on complete blood count?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Leukocyte count of 34,000/mm3 with lymphocyte predominance

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mild leukocytosis with a left shift

choices.label: C
choices.text: Leukopenia with relative lymphocytosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Normal leukocyte count with marked eosinophilia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Severe anemia with reticulocytosis

explanation.summary: This item tests expected laboratory findings in acute appendicitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mild leukocytosis with a left shift is present in most cases of acute appendicitis. Additional laboratory studies are used mainly to exclude other causes of pain such as gallstone complications, urinary tract infection, and ectopic pregnancy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A markedly elevated count with lymphocyte predominance is not characteristic of appendicitis, in which the elevation is mild and neutrophilic.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Correct: mild leukocytosis with a left shift is the typical finding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A lower leukocyte count with relative lymphocytosis is more characteristic of mesenteric adenitis, an important mimic of appendicitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Eosinophilia is not a described feature of acute appendicitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anemia is not expected in acute appendicitis; painless bleeding with iron deficiency anemia suggests angiodysplasia instead.

questions.stem: A hospital reviews the causes of acute abdominal pain among patients who required urgent abdominal surgery. Which of the following is the most common cause of acute abdominal pain requiring surgery?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute diverticulitis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Adhesive small bowel obstruction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sigmoid volvulus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Acute mesenteric ischemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Acute appendicitis

explanation.summary: This item tests the epidemiologic importance of appendicitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute appendicitis is the most common cause of acute abdominal pain requiring surgery, with a lifetime risk of approximately 7 to 9 percent and peak incidence in the second and third decades of life. Laparoscopic appendectomy is its definitive treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Most diverticulitis is uncomplicated and treated with antibiotics; only about 12 to 15 percent of cases are complicated and require drainage or surgery.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Adhesions are the most common cause of small bowel obstruction, but about 85 percent of adhesive obstructions resolve without surgery.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sigmoid volvulus is the most common benign cause of colonic obstruction and is initially treated with endoscopic decompression rather than surgery.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acute mesenteric ischemia is a highly lethal but far less common cause of acute abdominal pain.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Correct: acute appendicitis is the most common cause of acute abdominal pain requiring surgery.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of right lower quadrant abdominal pain and vomiting for 2 days. He had an upper respiratory infection the previous week. His temperature is 38.2 C (100.8 F). Abdominal tenderness is diffuse in the right lower quadrant, shifts when he changes position, and there is no rebound. Leukocyte count is 9,000/mm3 with relative lymphocytosis. Ultrasonography shows a cluster of enlarged right lower quadrant lymph nodes and a normal appendix. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute appendicitis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ileocolic intussusception

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mesenteric adenitis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Necrotizing enterocolitis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ischemic colitis

explanation.summary: This item tests recognition of the leading mimic of appendicitis in children.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mesenteric adenitis is inflammation of mesenteric lymph nodes, usually triggered by a viral illness such as a preceding upper respiratory infection or by bacterial enteritis. Tenderness is less localized and may shift with repositioning, peritoneal signs are less common, and labs show a lower leukocyte count with relative lymphocytosis. Imaging showing enlarged right lower quadrant nodes with a normal appendix confirms it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Appendicitis would show a dilated, inflamed appendix on imaging rather than a normal appendix, and would typically produce neutrophilic leukocytosis with localized tenderness.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Intussusception peaks at 5 to 9 months and presents with colicky pain, currant jelly stool, and a target sign on ultrasonography.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Correct: enlarged clustered mesenteric nodes with a normal appendix, shifting tenderness, and lymphocytosis define mesenteric adenitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Necrotizing enterocolitis occurs in preterm neonates in the first weeks of life, not in school-age children.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ischemic colitis predominantly affects the elderly and causes abdominal pain followed by hematochezia.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old woman has had periumbilical abdominal pain for 8 hours that is now shifting toward the right lower quadrant. Which of the following additional historical features is most likely to be present?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anorexia that began after the pain

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bloody diarrhea within 24 hours of pain onset

choices.label: C
choices.text: Painless, brisk rectal bleeding

choices.label: D
choices.text: Projectile nonbilious vomiting for several weeks

choices.label: E
choices.text: Postprandial pain relieved by lying prone

explanation.summary: This item tests the symptom sequence in acute appendicitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Anorexia occurs in about 85 percent of patients with appendicitis and characteristically follows rather than precedes the onset of pain. Nausea and vomiting may also occur, and pain migrates to the right lower quadrant within 24 hours in most patients.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Correct: anorexia is present in most patients and typically follows the onset of pain.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Abdominal pain followed by hematochezia or bloody diarrhea within 24 hours characterizes ischemic colitis in elderly patients.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Painless brisk hematochezia is characteristic of diverticular bleeding from arterial rupture at a diverticular neck.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Progressive projectile nonbilious vomiting at 3 to 6 weeks of age describes infantile pyloric stenosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Postprandial pain that improves in the prone or left lateral decubitus position describes superior mesenteric artery syndrome.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man has uncomplicated acute appendicitis. CT shows a mildly inflamed appendix without an appendicolith, mass, or marked dilation. He wishes to avoid an operation and elects nonoperative treatment with antibiotics alone. He should be counseled that approximately what proportion of similar patients will have recurrent appendicitis requiring surgery within 90 days?

explanation.summary: This item tests counseling for an antibiotics-first strategy in uncomplicated appendicitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: An antibiotics-first, nonsurgical approach is a viable alternative in selected patients with uncomplicated appendicitis, with outcomes comparable to appendectomy. However, approximately 30 percent of these patients have recurrence within 90 days that requires surgery. Guidelines support offering antibiotics only to patients without high-risk CT findings.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This understates the recurrence risk of nonoperative management by a wide margin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A 5 percent figure would misrepresent nonoperative therapy as nearly definitive.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This still substantially underestimates the reported 90-day recurrence rate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Correct: about 30 percent of patients treated with antibiotics alone recur within 90 days and require surgery.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A majority-failure rate would make antibiotics an unacceptable alternative, which is not the case.

questions.stem: A surgeon classifies patients with acute appendicitis as having either uncomplicated or complicated disease. Which of the following features defines complicated appendicitis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Perforation with abscess or phlegmon

choices.label: B
choices.text: Symptom duration longer than 24 hours

choices.label: C
choices.text: Appendiceal diameter greater than 6 mm on CT

choices.label: D
choices.text: Presence of an appendicolith

choices.label: E
choices.text: Leukocyte count above 12,000/mm3 with a left shift

explanation.summary: This item tests the definition of complicated versus uncomplicated appendicitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Uncomplicated appendicitis has no perforation, abscess, or phlegmon, whereas complicated appendicitis is defined by perforation with abscess or phlegmon. This distinction drives management, including the need for drainage and for postoperative antibiotics.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Correct: perforation with abscess or phlegmon defines complicated appendicitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Symptoms lasting more than 24 hours increase the risk of perforation but do not by themselves classify the disease as complicated.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Appendiceal dilation greater than 6 mm is a diagnostic CT criterion for appendicitis and is present in uncomplicated disease as well.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An appendicolith is a high-risk feature that argues against nonoperative therapy but is not part of the complicated definition.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mild leukocytosis with a left shift occurs in most cases of appendicitis, including uncomplicated disease.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man has 2 days of steadily worsening left lower quadrant abdominal pain. His temperature is 38.3 C (100.9 F). Examination shows focal left lower quadrant tenderness without rebound. Leukocyte count is 14,500/mm3. He has had no rectal bleeding. CT of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast shows thickening of a segment of the sigmoid colon with surrounding pericolic fat stranding and numerous adjacent outpouchings. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Angiodysplasia of the right colon

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ischemic colitis of the splenic flexure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Acute sigmoid diverticulitis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sigmoid volvulus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Obstructing carcinoma of the descending colon

explanation.summary: Classic presentation and CT appearance of acute uncomplicated diverticulitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Left lower quadrant pain with fever, leukocytosis, and focal left lower quadrant tenderness is the classic triad of acute diverticulitis, which in Western populations is predominantly sigmoid. CT with intravenous contrast is the gold standard, and it shows exactly what is described here: inflammation and wall thickening of a diverticula-bearing sigmoid segment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Angiodysplasia produces painless bleeding, most often from the cecum and right colon, and does not cause fever, leukocytosis, or focal left lower quadrant inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ischemic colitis typically causes abdominal pain followed within 24 hours by hematochezia or bloody diarrhea; this patient has had no bleeding, and the inflamed segment contains diverticula.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Correct. Fever, leukocytosis, focal left lower quadrant tenderness, and CT showing sigmoid wall thickening with pericolic stranding among diverticula define acute diverticulitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sigmoid volvulus presents with obstruction, abdominal distension, and obstipation with a dilated coffee bean shaped loop, not focal inflammation of a diverticula-bearing segment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Colorectal carcinoma causes insidious obstruction with distension and obstipation rather than acute fever and focal pericolic inflammation over 2 days.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with 36 hours of left lower quadrant pain and fever. She is tender in the left lower quadrant, and her leukocyte count is 15,200/mm3. Acute diverticulitis is suspected clinically. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic study to confirm the diagnosis and assess for complications?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Colonoscopy during the acute presentation

choices.label: B
choices.text: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast

choices.label: C
choices.text: Supine and upright plain abdominal radiographs

choices.label: D
choices.text: CT angiography of the mesenteric vessels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transabdominal ultrasonography of the right lower quadrant

explanation.summary: CT with intravenous contrast is the gold standard test for acute diverticulitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast is the gold standard for diagnosing diverticulitis. It confirms the inflamed segment and identifies the complications that change management, such as abscess, perforation, fistula, obstruction, or stricture.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Colonoscopy is useful for evaluating luminal lesions such as a narrowed segment after recovery, not for establishing the diagnosis during acute inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Correct. CT with intravenous contrast is the gold standard and distinguishes uncomplicated disease from abscess, perforation, fistula, obstruction, or stricture.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Plain films are used to demonstrate bowel obstruction patterns and free air; they cannot show pericolic inflammation or an abscess.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CT angiography is the test of choice for acute mesenteric ischemia, which presents with pain out of proportion to examination, not focal left lower quadrant inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ultrasonography of the right lower quadrant is used in children and pregnant patients evaluated for appendicitis, not for suspected sigmoid diverticulitis.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man undergoes screening colonoscopy that shows numerous outpouchings throughout the sigmoid colon. Histologic examination of a resected specimen from a similar patient shows that these outpouchings are pseudodiverticula. Which of the following components of the bowel wall makes up these lesions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All layers of the bowel wall, including muscularis propria and serosa

choices.label: B
choices.text: Muscularis propria and serosa only

choices.label: C
choices.text: Serosa only

choices.label: D
choices.text: Submucosa and muscularis propria

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mucosa and submucosa only

explanation.summary: Colonic diverticula are pseudodiverticula containing only mucosa and submucosa.
explanation.whyCorrect: Colonic diverticula are outpouchings of mucosa and submucosa that herniate through the muscular layer of the wall. Because they do not contain all layers, they are termed pseudodiverticula.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A true diverticulum containing all layers is not what forms in the colon; colonic diverticula herniate through the muscular layer rather than including it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The muscularis propria is the layer through which the mucosa and submucosa herniate, so it does not form the wall of the pouch.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The serosa is not the structural component of these outpouchings; the herniating tissue is mucosa and submucosa.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The submucosa herniates, but it does so together with the mucosa and through, not with, the muscularis propria.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Correct. Colonic pseudodiverticula are composed of mucosa and submucosa that herniate through the muscular layer.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman with extensive colonic diverticulosis asks why the pouches form in specific spots along the bowel rather than randomly. Colonic diverticula characteristically herniate at which of the following sites?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Points where penetrating vasa recta traverse the muscular wall near the tenia coli

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mucosal lymphoid aggregates that weaken the overlying epithelium

choices.label: C
choices.text: The antimesenteric border midway between the tenia, where epiploic appendages attach

choices.label: D
choices.text: Segments where the outer longitudinal muscle layer is continuous and complete

choices.label: E
choices.text: The line of insertion of the mesocolon along the mesenteric border

explanation.summary: Diverticula form at anatomic weak points created by penetrating blood vessels.
explanation.whyCorrect: Diverticula herniate through the muscular layer at the sites where the vasa recta penetrate the colonic wall near the tenia coli. These vascular entry points are structural weak spots, which also explains why diverticular hemorrhage arises from an artery at the neck of the pouch.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Correct. Penetrating vasa recta create defects in the muscular wall near the tenia coli through which mucosa and submucosa herniate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphoid hyperplasia acts as a lead point or luminal obstruction in other conditions; it is not the site of diverticular herniation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Epiploic appendages are surface structures and do not define the point of herniation; the vascular penetration sites near the tenia do.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Where the longitudinal muscle layer is complete, as in the rectum, diverticula do not form at all.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The pouches are related to the vascular penetration points rather than to the mesocolic insertion line itself.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man undergoes colonoscopy that shows extensive diverticula in the sigmoid and descending colon. The rectum is entirely free of diverticula. Which of the following best explains why the rectum is spared?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The rectum lacks a submucosal layer

choices.label: B
choices.text: Stool in the rectum is never firm enough to raise wall pressure

choices.label: C
choices.text: The tenia converge in the rectum to create a complete outer longitudinal muscle layer

choices.label: D
