questions.stem: A 44-year-old man is seen 1 week after outpatient repair of a symptomatic inguinal hernia. His pain is well controlled and the wound is healing normally. He asks when he can resume lifting weights at the gym. Which of the following is the most appropriate advice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: There are no activity restrictions after hernia repair

choices.label: B
choices.text: Avoid lifting more than 10 to 15 pounds for 1 week only

choices.label: C
choices.text: Avoid all physical activity for 6 months

choices.label: D
choices.text: Avoid lifting more than 10 to 15 pounds for 4 to 6 weeks

choices.label: E
choices.text: Maintain strict bed rest for 2 weeks, then resume all activity

explanation.summary: Postoperative activity guidance protects the repair during early healing.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most hernia repairs are performed as outpatient procedures with rapid recovery, and patients are typically advised to avoid heavy lifting of more than 10 to 15 pounds for 4 to 6 weeks after repair. Postoperative management focuses on pain control, activity guidance, and complication prevention.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Unrestricted lifting in the early postoperative period stresses the healing repair.
whyWrongByChoice.B: One week is too short; the recommended restriction lasts 4 to 6 weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Six months of complete inactivity is far beyond the recommended restriction and conflicts with rapid recovery after outpatient repair.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Correct: avoid lifting more than 10 to 15 pounds for 4 to 6 weeks after repair.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Strict bed rest is not advised; early mobilization with a limit on heavy lifting is standard.

questions.topicName: Hernias: Types, Risk Factors and Management
questions.stem: A 79-year-old man with a symptomatic, reducible inguinal hernia asks whether he can simply wear a truss instead of having an operation. Which of the following best describes the principal limitation of this approach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It does not correct the underlying defect and may cause tissue atrophy

choices.label: B
choices.text: It eliminates the risk of strangulation but not the risk of recurrence

choices.label: C
choices.text: It reliably provides complete containment of the hernia contents during activity

choices.label: D
choices.text: It accelerates spontaneous closure of the fascial defect

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is contraindicated in all patients because it raises intra-abdominal pressure to dangerous levels

explanation.summary: External supports are temporizing devices, not definitive treatment.
explanation.whyCorrect: Trusses and binders are historical approaches largely supplanted by modern surgical techniques and should be used only as a temporary measure. They rarely provide complete containment, may cause tissue damage or atrophy with prolonged use, and do not address the underlying anatomical defect; surgical repair remains the definitive treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Correct: a truss neither corrects the defect nor is safe for prolonged use.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A truss does not eliminate the risk of strangulation, since the defect and its contents remain.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Trusses rarely provide complete containment of hernia contents.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Adult fascial defects do not close spontaneously, and an external support does not promote closure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trusses are not avoided because they raise intra-abdominal pressure; they are avoided because they are ineffective and can damage tissue.

questions.topicName: Hernias: Types, Risk Factors and Management
questions.stem: A 22-year-old man has had an intermittent right groin bulge since childhood that enlarges with straining and descends into the scrotum. At operation, the sac is found to enter the internal inguinal ring and travel within the spermatic cord. Which of the following mechanisms best explains this hernia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acquired weakness of the posterior wall of the inguinal canal

choices.label: B
choices.text: Widening of the femoral canal medial to the femoral vein

choices.label: C
choices.text: Failure of umbilical ring closure with increased intra-abdominal pressure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Failure of fascial healing at a prior surgical incision

choices.label: E
choices.text: Persistence of the processus vaginalis

explanation.summary: Indirect inguinal hernias arise from a congenital patent pathway rather than acquired wall weakness.
explanation.whyCorrect: Indirect inguinal hernias result from a persistent processus vaginalis, allowing contents to enter the internal ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels and follow the spermatic cord. This explains the lifelong history and the descent into the scrotum in a young man.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acquired weakness of the posterior canal wall produces a direct hernia, which is typically seen in older adults and rarely reaches the scrotum.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Widening of the femoral canal produces a femoral hernia, which lies below the inguinal ligament and never enters the scrotum.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Failure of umbilical ring closure produces an umbilical hernia at the navel.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Failure of fascial healing at an incision produces an incisional hernia, and this patient has no prior operation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Correct: a persistent processus vaginalis underlies the indirect inguinal hernia described.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man reports 3 months of bright red blood dripping into the toilet bowl after bowel movements. The blood is not mixed into the stool, and the episodes are painless. He eats little fiber and strains to pass stool. On examination, straining produces a small mass of tissue at the anus that is covered by glistening mucosa; it slides back inside on its own when he stops straining. Digital rectal examination causes no significant pain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anal fissure

choices.label: B
choices.text: Prolapsing internal hemorrhoid

choices.label: C
choices.text: Thrombosed external hemorrhoid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Perianal abscess

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fistula-in-ano

explanation.summary: Painless bright red bleeding separate from stool with mucosa-covered tissue that prolapses and reduces spontaneously is classic for internal hemorrhoidal disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Internal hemorrhoids arise above the dentate line and are covered by viscerally innervated columnar mucosa, so they bleed painlessly and the blood typically appears separate from the stool, such as dripping into the bowl. As the supporting connective tissue degrades, they prolapse with straining; here the prolapsed tissue is mucosa-covered and painless on manipulation, matching an internal hemorrhoid.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An anal fissure is a tear in the somatically innervated anoderm and causes sharp, tearing pain with defecation, not painless bleeding with a reducible mucosa-covered mass.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Correct. Painless bright red bleeding separate from stool plus mucosa-covered tissue that prolapses with straining and reduces spontaneously defines symptomatic internal hemorrhoids.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A thrombosed external hemorrhoid presents as sudden severe perianal pain with a firm, tender, bluish lump at the anal verge covered by skin, not painless mucosa-covered prolapse.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A perianal abscess causes constant throbbing pain with swelling, erythema, and sometimes fever; this patient has no pain and no inflammatory findings.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A fistula-in-ano presents with persistent or recurrent drainage from a small opening near the anus, not painless bleeding with reducible prolapse.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman has 6 weeks of painless bright red rectal bleeding on the toilet tissue. Anoscopy shows engorged vascular cushions located above the dentate line, covered by columnar mucosa. Which of the following best explains why her hemorrhoidal disease is painless?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tissue above the dentate line has visceral innervation, which is insensate to sharp pain

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tissue above the dentate line is supplied by the pudendal nerve, which carries only motor fibers

choices.label: C
choices.text: The overlying skin protects the tissue from painful traumatic injury

choices.label: D
choices.text: Chronic relaxation of the internal anal sphincter prevents painful spasm

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrombosis within the cushions blocks conduction in adjacent somatic sensory nerve endings

explanation.summary: The dentate line separates viscerally innervated mucosa above from somatically innervated squamous epithelium below, which explains painless internal hemorrhoidal bleeding.
explanation.whyCorrect: Above the dentate line the canal is lined by endoderm-derived columnar mucosa with visceral innervation that registers stretch and pressure but not sharp pain. That is why internal hemorrhoids bleed painlessly, while the somatically innervated tissue below the dentate line makes thrombosed external hemorrhoids acutely painful.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Correct. Visceral innervation above the dentate line transmits stretch and pressure but not sharp pain, so internal hemorrhoids bleed without pain.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The pudendal nerve (S2–S4) supplies the region below the dentate line and carries exquisite sensitivity to pain, temperature, and touch; it does not explain painlessness above the line.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Skin covering applies to external hemorrhoids below the dentate line; the tissue described here is covered by columnar mucosa, which is friable and prone to bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sphincter spasm relates to the pain of anal fissures; it is not the reason internal hemorrhoidal bleeding is painless.
whyWrongByChoice.E: There is no thrombosis in this patient, and thrombosis in hemorrhoidal tissue produces pain rather than eliminating it.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman is evaluated for an intermittent lump at the anus. Examination identifies an external hemorrhoid. Which of the following best describes the location, covering, and sensation of this structure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Above the dentate line, covered with mucosa, visceral sensation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Above the dentate line, covered with skin, somatic sensation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Below the dentate line, covered with mucosa, visceral sensation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Below the dentate line, covered with skin, somatic sensation

choices.label: E
choices.text: At the anorectal junction, covered with mucosa, somatic sensation

explanation.summary: External hemorrhoids arise below the dentate line and are covered by somatically innervated squamous epithelium (skin).
explanation.whyCorrect: The dentate line divides the anal canal; below it the lining is ectoderm-derived squamous epithelium with somatic innervation from the pudendal nerve. External hemorrhoids therefore lie below the dentate line, are covered by skin, and are exquisitely sensitive to pain, temperature, and touch.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This describes an internal hemorrhoid, which arises above the dentate line under columnar mucosa with visceral sensation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Tissue above the dentate line is covered by mucosa and has visceral, not somatic, sensation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Below the dentate line the covering is squamous epithelium (skin) with somatic sensation, not mucosa with visceral sensation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Correct. External hemorrhoids arise below the dentate line, are covered by skin, and carry somatic sensation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The anorectal junction is where the rectum passes through the levator ani at the top of the canal, well above where external hemorrhoids arise, and that zone has visceral sensation.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman presents with 2 days of sudden, severe, constant perianal pain that began after several days of constipation and straining. She has had no fever, drainage, or bleeding. On examination there is a firm, exquisitely tender, 1-cm bluish lump at the anal verge covered by intact skin. There is no surrounding cellulitis and no fluctuance. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Prolapsing grade III internal hemorrhoid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Perianal abscess

choices.label: C
choices.text: Thrombosed external hemorrhoid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Chronic anal fissure

choices.label: E
choices.text: Squamous cell carcinoma of the anal canal

explanation.summary: A firm, tender, bluish, skin-covered lump at the anal verge with abrupt severe pain is a thrombosed external hemorrhoid.
explanation.whyCorrect: External hemorrhoids lie below the dentate line under somatically innervated skin and are usually asymptomatic until they thrombose. Acute thrombosis produces sudden, severe perianal pain with a firm, tender, bluish lump at the anal verge, exactly as described here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A grade III internal hemorrhoid is mucosa-covered prolapsing tissue that requires manual reduction and bleeds painlessly; it does not present as a firm bluish skin-covered lump with severe pain.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A perianal abscess causes constant throbbing pain with erythema, swelling, fluctuance, and sometimes fever; this lesion is bluish and skin-covered without inflammatory signs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Correct. Sudden severe pain with a firm, tender, bluish lump at the anal verge covered by skin is the classic presentation of a thrombosed external hemorrhoid.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A chronic anal fissure is a posterior midline tear with a sentinel tag, causing sharp tearing pain during defecation rather than a discrete bluish mass.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anal cancer presents as a hard, fixed, or ulcerated mass that fails to resolve, not as a lesion of 2 days' duration arising abruptly after straining.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man has had severe perianal pain for 2 days, rated 9 out of 10 and poorly controlled with acetaminophen. Examination shows a firm, tender, bluish 1.5-cm lump at the anal verge covered by intact skin, consistent with a thrombosed external hemorrhoid. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Excision of the thrombosed external hemorrhoid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rubber band ligation of the lesion in the office

choices.label: C
choices.text: Incision of the lesion to express the clot

choices.label: D
choices.text: Topical hydrocortisone suppositories to shrink the lesion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lateral internal sphincterotomy

explanation.summary: Thrombosed external hemorrhoids with severe pain are best excised within 3–4 days of symptom onset.
explanation.whyCorrect: Excision of a thrombosed external hemorrhoid within 3–4 days of symptom onset provides faster relief when pain is severe, and it can be performed under local anesthetic. This patient is on day 2 with severe uncontrolled pain, so he falls squarely within the window in which excision is beneficial.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Correct. Within 3–4 days of onset, excision under local anesthetic gives faster relief of severe pain from a thrombosed external hemorrhoid.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Rubber band ligation is an office procedure for symptomatic internal hemorrhoids placed above the dentate line; banding somatically innervated tissue at the anal verge is not the treatment here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Simple incision to remove the clot is not as effective as excision, which is the preferred procedure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Topical ointments and suppositories do not shrink hemorrhoidal tissue and would not relieve severe pain from an acute thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lateral internal sphincterotomy treats chronic anal fissures refractory to medical therapy, not thrombosed external hemorrhoids.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman has had a painful perianal lump for 8 days. The pain peaked on day 2 and has steadily improved over the past 3 days; she now takes no analgesics. Examination shows a firm bluish lump at the anal verge covered by intact skin, mildly tender, with no erythema or drainage. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Excision of the lesion in the office under local anesthetic

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conservative management with fiber, fluids, and sitz baths

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rubber band ligation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Excisional hemorrhoidectomy in the operating room under general anesthesia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Incision and evacuation of the clot

explanation.summary: After the first 3–4 days, thrombosed external hemorrhoids are managed conservatively because symptoms are already resolving.
explanation.whyCorrect: The benefit of excising a thrombosed external hemorrhoid is limited to roughly the first 3–4 days of symptoms, when pain is severe. Beyond that period symptoms typically improve on their own and procedural pain may prolong recovery, so conservative management is preferred; thrombosed hemorrhoids resolve over the course of a couple of weeks.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Excision is beneficial within 3–4 days of onset; at day 8 with improving pain, the procedure risks prolonging recovery.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Correct. Past the early window, symptoms are already resolving and conservative measures are preferred.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rubber band ligation is used for symptomatic internal hemorrhoids above the dentate line, not for a skin-covered thrombosed external hemorrhoid.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemorrhoidectomy is reserved for grade III–IV or mixed hemorrhoidal disease refractory to less invasive treatment, not a resolving single thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Incision to remove clot is less effective than excision, and no procedure is indicated at this point in the natural history.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man reports painless bright red bleeding with bowel movements. He states that with each bowel movement a lump protrudes from the anus and stays out until he pushes it back in with his finger. On examination the protruding tissue is covered with mucosa and is not tender. Which of the following best characterizes the grade of his internal hemorrhoidal disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Grade I — bleeding without prolapse

choices.label: B
choices.text: Grade II — prolapse with straining that reduces spontaneously

choices.label: C
choices.text: Grade III — prolapse that requires manual reduction

choices.label: D
choices.text: Grade IV — prolapse that is irreducible

choices.label: E
choices.text: Grade III — prolapse that is irreducible

explanation.summary: Internal hemorrhoid grading tracks prolapse behavior; tissue that must be pushed back manually is grade III.
explanation.whyCorrect: Grade I hemorrhoids bleed but do not prolapse, grade II prolapse and reduce spontaneously, grade III prolapse and require manual reduction, and grade IV prolapse and are irreducible. This patient must manually reduce the prolapsed mucosa-covered tissue, which defines grade III.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Grade I is correctly defined here, but this patient clearly prolapses, so the grade does not fit.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Grade II is correctly defined, but his prolapse does not reduce on its own — he must push it back.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Correct. Prolapse requiring manual reduction is grade III.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Grade IV is correctly defined, but his prolapse is reducible with his finger, so it is not irreducible.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This pairs the wrong definition with grade III; irreducible prolapse is grade IV.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman has chronically prolapsed hemorrhoidal tissue that cannot be pushed back into the anal canal. She has taken fiber supplements and increased fluids for 6 months and has undergone two office procedures without improvement; she continues to have bleeding and soiling. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Continue fiber and fluids alone for another 6 months

choices.label: B
choices.text: Topical nitroglycerin ointment

choices.label: C
choices.text: Incision and drainage

choices.label: D
choices.text: Topical hydrocortisone suppositories

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hemorrhoidectomy under anesthesia

explanation.summary: Hemorrhoidectomy is reserved for grade III–IV disease or mixed hemorrhoidal disease refractory to less invasive treatment.
explanation.whyCorrect: Irreducible prolapse is grade IV disease. She has already failed conservative therapy and office-based treatment, and hemorrhoidectomy — an operative procedure under anesthetic that removes both internal and external hemorrhoidal tissue — is the appropriate treatment for grade III–IV or refractory disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dietary fiber and fluids are first-line therapy, but she has already failed 6 months of conservative management with ongoing symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Topical nitroglycerin relaxes internal sphincter spasm and is used for anal fissures, not for irreducible hemorrhoidal prolapse.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Incision and drainage treats a perianal abscess; there is no abscess here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Topical ointments and suppositories do not shrink hemorrhoidal tissue and would not address grade IV prolapse.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Correct. Grade IV prolapse refractory to conservative and office-based treatment is an indication for operative hemorrhoidectomy.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man has intermittent painless bright red bleeding on the toilet tissue. Anoscopy shows internal hemorrhoids that bleed but do not prolapse. He reports spending 20–30 minutes on the commode reading and straining at each bowel movement, and his diet is low in fiber. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rubber band ligation of the internal hemorrhoid columns in the office setting

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excisional hemorrhoidectomy under general anesthesia in the operating room

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased dietary fiber and fluids with less straining and commode time

choices.label: D
choices.text: Topical nifedipine ointment applied twice daily

choices.label: E
choices.text: Topical mesalamine suppositories at bedtime

explanation.summary: First-line therapy for all hemorrhoidal disease is increased dietary fiber and fluids plus bowel-habit modification.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hemorrhoidal disease most often results from increased venous pressure caused by chronic straining and a low-fiber diet. First-line treatment for all hemorrhoids is increased dietary fiber and adequate fluid intake, with patients advised to limit time on the commode to about 5 minutes and avoid straining — precisely the behaviors this patient reports.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Rubber band ligation is reserved for symptomatic internal hemorrhoids that do not respond to conservative measures, which he has not yet tried.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemorrhoidectomy is reserved for grade III–IV or mixed disease refractory to less invasive treatment; his hemorrhoids do not even prolapse.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Correct. Fiber, fluids, limiting commode time, and avoiding straining are first-line therapy for all hemorrhoids.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Topical calcium channel blockers such as nifedipine relax internal sphincter spasm in anal fissures; they are not hemorrhoid therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Topical mesalamine is first-line for ulcerative proctitis, which causes rectal bleeding with urgency and tenesmus, not for hemorrhoids.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman has had bleeding from internal hemorrhoids for 4 months. Despite 3 months of high-fiber diet, adequate fluids, limiting time on the commode, and avoiding straining, she continues to have bright red bleeding and tissue that prolapses with defecation and reduces on its own. Colonoscopy performed for the bleeding was normal apart from internal hemorrhoids. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Excision under local anesthetic

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lateral internal sphincterotomy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Over-the-counter topical ointment to shrink the hemorrhoids

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rubber band ligation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oral antibiotics

explanation.summary: Rubber band ligation is the most effective office-based procedure for symptomatic internal hemorrhoids that fail conservative therapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: When bleeding or prolapsing internal hemorrhoids do not respond to conservative measures, rubber band ligation is the most effective office-based procedure. This patient has documented internal hemorrhoids, a negative colonoscopy, and persistent symptoms after an adequate trial of fiber and bowel-habit modification.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Excision under local anesthetic is the treatment for an acutely thrombosed external hemorrhoid within 3–4 days of onset, not for bleeding internal hemorrhoids.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lateral internal sphincterotomy reduces resting internal sphincter tone in refractory chronic anal fissures; it does not treat hemorrhoidal bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Topical ointments and suppositories do not shrink hemorrhoidal tissue; at best they give minimal temporary relief of external discomfort.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Correct. Rubber band ligation is the most effective office procedure for symptomatic internal hemorrhoids refractory to conservative measures.
whyWrongByChoice.E: There is no infection here; antibiotics have no role in hemorrhoidal bleeding.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man is scheduled for office-based rubber band ligation of bleeding internal hemorrhoids. He asks whether he will need anesthesia or sedation for the procedure. The physician explains that the band will be placed at a specific level within the anal canal. Which of the following best explains why no anesthetic is required?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The band is placed at the anal verge, where the corrugator cutis ani muscle blocks sensation

choices.label: B
choices.text: The band is placed above the dentate line, where the tissue is minimally sensate

choices.label: C
choices.text: The band is placed below the dentate line, where squamous epithelium resists painful stimuli

choices.label: D
choices.text: The pudendal nerve does not supply any portion of the anal canal

choices.label: E
choices.text: The internal anal sphincter is divided first, eliminating pain transmission

explanation.summary: Rubber band ligation is performed without anesthetic because bands are applied above the dentate line, where innervation is visceral and the tissue is minimally sensate.
explanation.whyCorrect: Internal hemorrhoids lie above the dentate line under viscerally innervated columnar mucosa, which senses stretch and pressure but not sharp pain. Because that tissue is minimally sensate, a tight band can be applied around the hemorrhoidal pedicle in the office without anesthetic.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The anal verge is below the dentate line and is somatically innervated and highly pain sensitive; banding there would be painful.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Correct. Bands are placed above the dentate line on minimally sensate, viscerally innervated tissue, so no anesthetic is needed.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Squamous epithelium below the dentate line is exquisitely sensitive to pain, temperature, and touch, so it does not resist painful stimuli.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The pudendal nerve (S2–S4) does supply the anal canal below the dentate line; it simply is not the territory being banded.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dividing the internal sphincter describes lateral internal sphincterotomy for anal fissure and is not part of rubber band ligation.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman with prolapsing, bleeding internal hemorrhoids undergoes placement of a tight rubber band around the base of the hemorrhoidal tissue in the office. Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which this procedure relieves her symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The band relaxes internal anal sphincter tone, improving blood flow to the anoderm

choices.label: B
choices.text: The band evacuates thrombus from the hemorrhoidal cushion

choices.label: C
choices.text: The band closes the internal opening of an anal gland tract

choices.label: D
choices.text: The band physically reduces prolapsed tissue back above the levator ani

choices.label: E
choices.text: The banded tissue sloughs and scars, fixing the mucosa in place

explanation.summary: Rubber band ligation works by strangulating hemorrhoidal tissue so it necroses and sloughs, leaving fibrosis that fixes the mucosa in place.
explanation.whyCorrect: A tight band placed around the hemorrhoidal tissue above the dentate line causes that tissue to necrose and slough. Healing occurs with fibrosis that anchors the mucosa, which addresses both bleeding and prolapse.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Reducing internal sphincter tone is the goal of topical calcium channel blockers, nitroglycerin, and sphincterotomy for anal fissures, not of banding.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Clot evacuation applies to excision of a thrombosed external hemorrhoid; banding does not remove thrombus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Closing an anal gland tract relates to treatment of fistula-in-ano, a different disease process.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The band does not mechanically push tissue above the levator ani; the durable effect comes from necrosis followed by fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Correct. The ligated tissue necroses and sloughs, and healing produces fibrosis that anchors the mucosa.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man reports 2 months of rectal bleeding in which blood is mixed throughout the stool. He has also had looser stools than usual and has lost 5 kg. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin of 10.1 g/dL with a mean corpuscular volume of 76 fL and low ferritin. Anoscopy demonstrates small internal hemorrhoids. He has never undergone colorectal cancer screening. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Colonoscopy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rubber band ligation of the internal hemorrhoids

choices.label: C
choices.text: High-fiber diet and reassurance that the bleeding is hemorrhoidal

choices.label: D
choices.text: Topical hydrocortisone suppositories

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hemorrhoidectomy

explanation.summary: Rectal bleeding with atypical features, anemia, weight loss, or unmet screening requires colonoscopy — the presence of hemorrhoids does not exclude proximal pathology.
explanation.whyCorrect: Blood mixed with stool rather than on its surface, iron deficiency anemia, change in bowel habits, and weight loss are all indications for colonoscopy, as is age-appropriate need for colorectal cancer screening. Finding hemorrhoids does not exclude coexisting proximal disease, and attributing bleeding to hemorrhoids without evaluation is a common cause of delayed cancer diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Correct. Atypical bleeding, iron deficiency anemia, weight loss, altered bowel habits, and unmet screening all mandate colonoscopy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Banding treats symptomatic internal hemorrhoids but would leave a potential proximal source of bleeding uninvestigated.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reassurance without evaluation is exactly the error that leads to missed or delayed colorectal cancer diagnosis in this presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Topical products do not shrink hemorrhoidal tissue and do nothing to evaluate the alarm features present here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Operative hemorrhoidectomy is reserved for grade III–IV or refractory mixed disease and does not address the need for diagnostic evaluation.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man is referred for a "hemorrhoid that will not go away." He first noticed a perianal lump 4 months ago. On examination there is a firm, fixed, partially ulcerated reddish perianal mass that does not reduce and has not changed in size. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rubber band ligation of the mass

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sitz baths and reassurance that it will resolve within 2 weeks

choices.label: C
choices.text: Incision and drainage

choices.label: D
choices.text: Biopsy of the lesion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Topical hydrocortisone for 2 weeks

explanation.summary: A persistent, hard, fixed, or ulcerated perianal lesion is not a hemorrhoid and must be biopsied to exclude malignancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Thrombosed hemorrhoids resolve over the course of a couple of weeks, so a firm perianal mass present for 4 months is not a hemorrhoid even when patients and referring physicians call it one. Any external anal lesion that is hard, fixed, ulcerated, or fails to resolve should be biopsied to rule out malignancy, or referred to a surgeon for diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Banding is an office treatment for internal hemorrhoids above the dentate line and would treat an undiagnosed mass as benign.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reassurance is inappropriate because this lesion has already failed to resolve over 4 months, which argues strongly against a hemorrhoid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Incision and drainage treats a perianal abscess, which presents with throbbing pain, erythema, swelling, and often fever, not a chronic fixed ulcerated mass.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Correct. A hard, fixed, ulcerated, non-resolving perianal lesion requires biopsy to exclude malignancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Topical steroids treat perianal inflammation and itching and would only delay diagnosis of a possible cancer.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman is found to have a persistent ulcerated anal mass that had been assumed to be a hemorrhoid. Biopsy shows squamous cell carcinoma. Persistent infection with which of the following is most likely responsible for her malignancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2

choices.label: B
choices.text: Human papillomavirus 16 and 18

choices.label: C
choices.text: Treponema pallidum

choices.label: D
choices.text: Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1 to L3

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neisseria gonorrhoeae

explanation.summary: Anal cancers are squamous cell carcinomas driven by persistent HPV infection, with types 16 and 18 accounting for most cases.
explanation.whyCorrect: Anal cancer must be considered when an anal or perianal lesion behaves atypically for a hemorrhoid. These tumors are squamous cell carcinomas driven by persistent human papillomavirus infection, and HPV types 16 and 18 account for roughly 90% of cases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Herpes simplex virus is a cause of infectious proctitis with anorectal pain and discharge; it is not the driver of anal squamous cell carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Correct. Persistent HPV infection, particularly types 16 and 18, causes about 90% of anal squamous cell carcinomas.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Treponema pallidum causes infectious proctitis and should be considered for a non-midline fissure, but it does not cause anal squamous cell carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chlamydia trachomatis causes infectious proctitis diagnosed by nucleic acid amplification testing, not anal carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is another cause of infectious proctitis in patients with receptive anal intercourse, not of anal cancer.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man has excruciating pain from a thrombosed external hemorrhoid at the anal verge; even light touch during examination is intolerable. Sensation from which of the following is responsible for the severity of his pain?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Visceral afferents accompanying the pelvic splanchnic supply to the rectum

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sympathetic fibers traveling with the inferior mesenteric plexus

choices.label: C
choices.text: The pudendal nerve (S2–S4) supplying tissue below the dentate line

choices.label: D
choices.text: The levator ani motor supply at the anorectal junction

choices.label: E
choices.text: Visceral afferents in the columnar mucosa above the dentate line

explanation.summary: Tissue below the dentate line is somatically innervated by the pudendal nerve (S2–S4), which is why thrombosed external hemorrhoids are exquisitely painful.
explanation.whyCorrect: External hemorrhoids arise below the dentate line, where the squamous epithelium receives somatic innervation from the pudendal nerve (S2–S4) and is exquisitely sensitive to pain, temperature, and touch. Acute thrombosis in this territory produces sudden, severe perianal pain and marked tenderness.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Visceral afferent supply senses stretch and pressure but not sharp pain and pertains to the zone above the dentate line.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Autonomic fibers do not mediate the sharp, exquisitely localized pain of tissue below the dentate line.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Correct. Somatic innervation by the pudendal nerve (S2–S4) below the dentate line explains the severe pain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The levator ani forms the pelvic floor at the anorectal junction and its motor supply does not mediate perianal cutaneous pain.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Visceral afferents above the dentate line do not transmit sharp pain, which is why internal hemorrhoids bleed painlessly.

questions.stem: During anoscopy of a 46-year-old man with painless rectal bleeding, tissue is sampled from the anal canal 1 cm proximal to the dentate line. Which of the following is most likely to be found on histologic examination of this tissue?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Columnar mucosa of endodermal origin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Squamous epithelium of ectodermal origin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Keratinized skin with hair follicles and sweat glands

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transitional urothelium

choices.label: E
choices.text: Squamous epithelium of endodermal origin

explanation.summary: Above the dentate line the anal canal is lined by endoderm-derived columnar mucosa; below it the lining is ectoderm-derived squamous epithelium.
explanation.whyCorrect: The dentate line lies roughly halfway up the anal canal and divides two functionally distinct zones. Tissue 1 cm proximal to it lies above the line and is columnar mucosa of endodermal origin, with visceral innervation — the friable lining that makes internal hemorrhoids prone to painless bleeding.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Correct. Above the dentate line the lining is endoderm-derived columnar mucosa.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ectoderm-derived squamous epithelium lines the canal below the dentate line, not above it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Skin with adnexal structures is found at and beyond the anal verge, well distal to the sampled site.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Urothelium lines the urinary tract and is not found in the anal canal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The squamous lining of the anal canal is ectodermal and lies below the dentate line, so this combination does not describe the sampled site.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old truck driver develops bleeding and prolapse from internal hemorrhoids. His diet consists almost entirely of fast food with minimal fruits, vegetables, and whole grains, and he reports prolonged straining with hard stools. Which of the following best explains the development of his hemorrhoidal disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Obstruction of anal glands at the dentate line with spread of infection into surrounding tissue

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reflex internal sphincter spasm producing posterior midline anodermal ischemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Autoimmune inflammation limited to the rectal mucosa

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased venous pressure in the anal cushions from chronic straining

choices.label: E
choices.text: Persistent viral infection of the anal transition zone

explanation.summary: Hemorrhoidal disease arises when normal anal vascular cushions become engorged, prolapsed, or thrombosed, most often from increased venous pressure due to straining and low fiber intake.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hemorrhoids are normal vascular cushions of the anal canal. Disease develops when they become engorged, prolapsed, or thrombosed, most often from increased venous pressure caused by chronic straining or a low-fiber diet — exactly this patient's pattern of hard stools and prolonged straining.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Obstruction of the anal glands at the dentate line is the origin of perianal abscesses and fistulas, not of hemorrhoidal disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reflex sphincter spasm with posterior midline ischemia explains the poor healing of anal fissures, not hemorrhoidal engorgement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inflammation confined to the rectal mucosa describes ulcerative proctitis, which causes bleeding with urgency and tenesmus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Correct. Chronic straining and a low-fiber diet raise venous pressure in the anal cushions, producing engorgement, prolapse, or thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Persistent viral infection of the anal region relates to HPV-driven anal squamous cell carcinoma, not to hemorrhoidal disease.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman undergoing evaluation for rectal bleeding asks why everyone has hemorrhoids if they cause disease. She is told that hemorrhoids are normal structures of the anal canal. Which of the following best describes their normal physiologic role?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They secrete mucus that lubricates the passage of stool

choices.label: B
choices.text: They generate the resting tone that closes the anal canal at rest

choices.label: C
choices.text: They anchor the rectum to the levator ani during defecation

choices.label: D
choices.text: They sense the temperature of rectal contents

choices.label: E
choices.text: They are vascular cushions that contribute to continence

explanation.summary: Hemorrhoids are normal vascular cushions of the anal canal that contribute to continence; disease occurs only when they become engorged, prolapsed, or thrombosed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hemorrhoids are normal anatomic structures — vascular cushions within the anal canal that contribute to continence. Hemorrhoidal disease is the pathologic state that arises when these cushions become engorged, prolapsed, or thrombosed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mucus secretion is a property of the anal glands and rectal mucosa, not the function ascribed to the hemorrhoidal cushions.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Resting closure of the anal canal is primarily a function of the internal anal sphincter, whose tone is the target of fissure treatments.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The levator ani forms the pelvic floor at the anorectal junction; hemorrhoidal cushions do not anchor the rectum to it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Temperature sensation belongs to the somatically innervated anoderm below the dentate line, not to the vascular cushions themselves.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Correct. Hemorrhoids are normal vascular cushions of the anal canal that contribute to continence.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman with symptomatic hemorrhoids has used over-the-counter anti-hemorrhoidal ointments and suppositories daily for 3 months, hoping the products will make her hemorrhoids disappear. Her symptoms are unchanged. Which of the following statements about these topical products is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They eliminate the need for dietary modification when used daily

choices.label: B
choices.text: They eradicate internal hemorrhoids by inducing mucosal fibrosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: They do not shrink hemorrhoids and offer only temporary symptom relief

choices.label: D
choices.text: They are more effective than dietary fiber for reducing hemorrhoidal bleeding

choices.label: E
choices.text: They prevent thrombosis of external hemorrhoids when applied prophylactically

explanation.summary: Topical anti-hemorrhoidal ointments and suppositories do not shrink hemorrhoidal tissue and are not a substitute for fiber, fluids, and bowel-habit modification.
explanation.whyCorrect: Topical ointments and suppositories do not shrink hemorrhoidal tissue. They may provide minimal temporary relief of external discomfort, which is why her symptoms are unchanged after 3 months and why first-line therapy remains increased dietary fiber and fluids with avoidance of straining.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Increased dietary fiber and fluid intake remain first-line therapy for all hemorrhoids and are not replaced by topical products.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibrosis that anchors the mucosa is produced by rubber band ligation, not by topical preparations.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Correct. These products do not shrink hemorrhoidal tissue and provide at most minimal temporary relief of external discomfort.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fiber and fluids with bowel-habit modification are first-line; topical products have not been shown to be superior.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thrombosis is not prevented by topical preparations; it results from the underlying engorgement of the external hemorrhoidal cushion.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman has a 2-week history of severe, knifelike anal pain that begins with each bowel movement and lingers for an hour afterward. She notes a small streak of bright red blood on the toilet tissue. She has been constipated and recently passed a large, hard stool. Gentle retraction of the buttocks with eversion of the anal mucosa reveals a linear tear in the anoderm at the posterior midline. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Thrombosed external hemorrhoid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anal fissure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Perianal abscess

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fistula-in-ano

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prolapsing internal hemorrhoid

explanation.summary: Classic presentation of an anal fissure: a tear in the somatically innervated anoderm after passage of a hard stool.
explanation.whyCorrect: An anal fissure is a tear in the anoderm, most commonly in the posterior midline, and the initial tear is usually caused by passage of a hard stool. Because the anoderm below the dentate line has somatic innervation, fissures cause sharp, tearing pain during defecation with a small amount of bright red blood. The visualized linear posterior midline tear confirms the diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A thrombosed external hemorrhoid presents as a sudden, firm, tender bluish lump at the anal verge, not a linear tear in the anoderm, and its pain is constant rather than triggered by defecation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Correct: a posterior midline tear in the anoderm after a hard stool, with sharp defecation-related pain and scant bright red blood, is an anal fissure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A perianal abscess causes constant, throbbing pain with swelling, erythema, and sometimes fever, and is typically visible and palpable as a tender fluctuant mass rather than a mucosal tear.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fistula-in-ano causes persistent or recurrent drainage from a small opening near the anus, usually after a prior abscess; there is no drainage or external opening here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prolapsing internal hemorrhoids arise above the dentate line, are covered by viscerally innervated mucosa, and produce painless bleeding or a protruding mucosa-covered mass rather than sharp defecation pain.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man reports 3 weeks of tearing pain with defecation and blood on the toilet tissue after an episode of constipation. He is otherwise healthy, is not sexually active, and has no diarrhea, weight loss, or perianal drainage. An anal fissure is suspected. This lesion is most likely to be found at which of the following locations in the anal canal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Right lateral wall

choices.label: B
choices.text: Left lateral wall

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anterior midline

choices.label: D
choices.text: Posterior midline

choices.label: E
choices.text: Circumferentially at the level of the dentate line

explanation.summary: Tests the characteristic location of anal fissures.
explanation.whyCorrect: Approximately 85% of anal fissures occur in the posterior midline. The posterior midline also has the poorest blood supply in the anal canal, which contributes to the poor healing that characterizes fissures.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A lateral fissure is atypical and should prompt suspicion for an alternate etiology such as Crohn disease, HIV, syphilis, or anal cancer; it is not the expected location in an otherwise healthy patient.
whyWrongByChoice.B: As with a right lateral fissure, a left lateral location is off-midline and atypical, raising concern for a secondary cause rather than a simple fissure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anterior midline fissures do occur but are far less common than posterior midline fissures, which account for about 85% of cases.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Correct: about 85% of anal fissures occur in the posterior midline, the zone with the poorest anal canal blood supply.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fissures are focal tears of the anoderm below the dentate line, not circumferential lesions at the dentate line.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man has had painful defecation with scant bright red bleeding for 10 weeks. Examination shows a posterior midline fissure with a small skin tag at its distal end. He has already been taking a fiber supplement, a stool softener, and daily sitz baths for 6 weeks without relief. Which of the following topical medications is most appropriate to add?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mesalamine suppository

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hydrocortisone 1% ointment

choices.label: C
choices.text: Zinc oxide barrier ointment

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mupirocin ointment

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nifedipine ointment

explanation.summary: Pharmacologic therapy for anal fissure targets internal anal sphincter spasm.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both acute and chronic fissures can be treated with topical calcium channel blockers such as nifedipine or with topical nitroglycerin. These agents relax the internal sphincter spasm, improving pain control and healing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Topical mesalamine is first-line therapy for ulcerative proctitis, which presents with rectal bleeding, urgency, and tenesmus, not for a fissure caused by sphincter spasm.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Low-potency topical corticosteroid is used for short courses in pruritus ani to break the itch-scratch cycle; it does not relieve internal sphincter hypertonicity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Barrier ointments such as zinc oxide are used for moisture control in pruritus ani and do nothing for sphincter spasm or fissure healing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A topical antibiotic addresses neither the sphincter spasm nor the ischemia responsible for non-healing; fissures are not primarily infectious.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Correct: topical calcium channel blockers such as nifedipine relax the internal sphincter spasm that impairs fissure healing.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has had sharp pain with bowel movements and intermittent spotting of bright red blood for 4 months. Retraction of the buttocks reveals an ulcerated tear in the posterior midline anoderm. Which of the following additional findings is most likely on her examination?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A firm, bluish lump at the anal verge

choices.label: B
choices.text: An external opening on the perianal skin intermittently draining purulent material

choices.label: C
choices.text: A sentinel skin tag with internal sphincter fibers at the ulcer base

choices.label: D
choices.text: A mucosa-covered mass protruding from the anal canal that reduces spontaneously

choices.label: E
choices.text: A fluctuant, erythematous swelling 2 cm lateral to the anal verge

explanation.summary: Tests recognition of the features of a chronic anal fissure.
explanation.whyCorrect: A fissure present for more than 6 to 8 weeks is considered chronic and develops characteristic features: an external sentinel skin tag, a hypertrophied anal papilla internally, and visible internal sphincter fibers at the base of the ulcer. This patient's 4-month course fits a chronic fissure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A firm bluish lump at the anal verge describes a thrombosed external hemorrhoid, which causes sudden severe constant pain rather than a chronic ulcerated anoderm tear.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A draining external opening indicates fistula-in-ano, a chronic tract from prior cryptoglandular infection, not a feature of a chronic fissure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Correct: chronic fissures develop a sentinel skin tag, a hypertrophied anal papilla, and exposed internal sphincter fibers at the ulcer base.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Spontaneously reducing mucosa-covered prolapse describes grade II internal hemorrhoids, which are painless and unrelated to fissure chronicity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A fluctuant erythematous perianal swelling indicates a perianal abscess with constant throbbing pain, not the chronic changes of a fissure.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man has a 6-week history of pain with defecation. Examination shows an anal fissure located on the right lateral wall of the anal canal rather than in the midline. He also reports several months of intermittent nonbloody diarrhea and a 5-kg weight loss. Which of the following underlying conditions is most likely responsible for his fissure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ulcerative proctitis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Crohn disease

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enterobius vermicularis infection

choices.label: D
choices.text: Internal hemorrhoidal disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: Irritable bowel syndrome

explanation.summary: An off-midline fissure signals a secondary cause rather than simple trauma from hard stool.
explanation.whyCorrect: Anal fissures are usually in the posterior midline; a fissure not in the midline should raise suspicion for an alternate etiology such as Crohn disease, HIV, syphilis, or anal cancer. The accompanying chronic diarrhea and weight loss point to Crohn disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ulcerative proctitis is inflammation limited to the rectum presenting with rectal bleeding, urgency, and tenesmus; it is not a recognized cause of a lateral anal fissure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Correct: a fissure outside the midline suggests an alternate etiology such as Crohn disease, which also explains his chronic diarrhea and weight loss.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pinworm infection classically causes nocturnal perianal itching in school-age children and is diagnosed with the Scotch tape test; it does not cause lateral fissures.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Internal hemorrhoids arise above the dentate line and cause painless bleeding or prolapse; they do not produce lateral anoderm tears.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Irritable bowel syndrome is not among the causes of an atypically located fissure and does not explain weight loss.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man has 3 days of constant, throbbing perianal pain that is worse when sitting. His temperature is 38.2 C (100.8 F). Examination shows a tender, erythematous, fluctuant swelling 2 cm lateral to the anal verge. There is no bleeding with defecation and no chronic drainage. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Perianal abscess

choices.label: B
choices.text: Thrombosed external hemorrhoid

choices.label: C
choices.text: Acute anal fissure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fistula-in-ano

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prolapsed internal hemorrhoid

explanation.summary: Constant throbbing perianal pain with fever and a fluctuant, erythematous swelling is a perianal abscess.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with a perianal abscess present with constant, throbbing perianal pain, swelling, erythema, and sometimes fever, and the abscess is often visible and palpable on examination. Fluctuance is the classic physical exam descriptor for an abscess, reflecting a compressible fluid collection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Correct: fever plus a fluctuant, erythematous, tender perianal swelling with constant throbbing pain defines a perianal abscess.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A thrombosed external hemorrhoid is a firm bluish lump at the anal verge covered by skin; it is not fluctuant, erythematous, or febrile.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An acute fissure causes sharp tearing pain specifically during defecation with a small amount of bright red blood, and shows a tear in the anoderm rather than a fluctuant mass.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fistula-in-ano presents with persistent or recurrent drainage from a small opening near the anus, typically after a prior abscess, not with an acute undrained fluctuant swelling.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A prolapsed internal hemorrhoid is a mucosa-covered protrusion associated with painless bleeding, not a febrile fluctuant perianal mass.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old healthy woman has 4 days of increasing perianal pain and swelling. Examination shows a 3-cm tender, erythematous, fluctuant mass at the anal verge. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oral cephalexin and warm sitz baths without a procedure

choices.label: B
choices.text: Topical nitroglycerin ointment

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rubber band ligation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Incision and drainage

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fistulotomy

explanation.summary: The treatment of a perianal abscess is prompt drainage.
explanation.whyCorrect: Treatment of a perianal abscess is prompt incision and drainage. Source control, not medical therapy, resolves the collection, and delay allows the patient to become increasingly ill.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibiotics do not drain a fluid collection; they are reserved as an adjunct for surrounding cellulitis, systemic signs of infection, or immunosuppression, and never substitute for drainage.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Topical nitroglycerin relaxes internal sphincter spasm and is used for anal fissures; it has no role in an abscess.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rubber band ligation is the office procedure for symptomatic internal hemorrhoids above the dentate line, not for an infected fluid collection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Correct: prompt incision and drainage is the treatment of a perianal abscess.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fistulotomy treats an established simple, low fistula tract; there is no chronic tract here, only an acute undrained abscess.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old healthy man undergoes incision and drainage of a perianal abscess in the office. After drainage he is afebrile and comfortable. There is no surrounding cellulitis, and he takes no immunosuppressive medications and has no chronic illness. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A 7-day course of oral ciprofloxacin and metronidazole

choices.label: B
choices.text: Admission for intravenous antibiotics

choices.label: C
choices.text: Wound care and sitz baths without antibiotics

choices.label: D
choices.text: Topical nifedipine ointment

choices.label: E
choices.text: Immediate fistulotomy

explanation.summary: Antibiotics add nothing after adequate drainage of a perianal abscess in a healthy patient.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antibiotics are not needed in healthy patients because drainage alone is sufficient. Antibiotics are reserved for patients with surrounding cellulitis, systemic signs of infection, or immunosuppression, none of which is present here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Oral antibiotics are unnecessary in a healthy, afebrile patient without cellulitis whose abscess has been adequately drained.
whyWrongByChoice.B: There are no systemic signs of infection to justify intravenous antibiotics or admission after successful office drainage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Correct: drainage alone is sufficient in a healthy patient; local wound care and sitz baths are all that is required.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Topical calcium channel blockers relax internal sphincter spasm in anal fissures and have no role after abscess drainage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fistulotomy is reserved for an established simple, low fistula tract; a fistula may or may not develop and is not treated preemptively at the time of drainage.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man is diagnosed with a perianal abscess and asks how the infection started, since he has had no injury and no recent instrumentation. Which of the following best explains the origin of his abscess?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Obstruction of an anal gland at the dentate line with spread into adjacent spaces

choices.label: B
choices.text: Thrombosis of the external hemorrhoidal plexus with secondary necrosis of the overlying skin

choices.label: C
choices.text: A tear in the anoderm caused by passage of a hard stool

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hematogenous seeding of the ischioanal fat from a distant infection

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sexually transmitted infection of the rectal mucosa

explanation.summary: Perianal abscesses arise by the cryptoglandular mechanism.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most perianal abscesses originate from infection of the anal glands. These glands open into crypts at the dentate line and extend into the intersphincteric space; when they become obstructed, the resulting infection spreads into the surrounding anatomic spaces.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Correct: obstruction of a cryptoglandular anal gland at the dentate line with spread of infection is the origin of perianal abscesses.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Thrombosis of the external hemorrhoidal plexus produces a painful thrombosed external hemorrhoid, not a suppurative perianal collection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A tear in the anoderm from a hard stool is the mechanism of an anal fissure, which causes pain with defecation rather than an abscess.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Perianal abscesses arise locally from obstructed anal glands rather than from bloodborne seeding of the ischioanal fat.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sexually transmitted organisms cause infectious proctitis with anorectal pain, tenesmus, and mucopurulent discharge, not cryptoglandular abscess formation.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man underwent incision and drainage of a perianal abscess 6 weeks ago. His pain resolved, but he now reports continuous soiling of his underwear from a small opening in the skin near the anus. Examination shows a punctate external opening 2 cm from the anal verge that expresses a small amount of purulent material; there is no fluctuance, erythema, or fever. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anal fissure

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pruritus ani

choices.label: C
choices.text: Recurrent undrained perianal abscess

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thrombosed external hemorrhoid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fistula-in-ano

explanation.summary: Persistent drainage from a small perianal opening after an abscess is a fistula-in-ano.
explanation.whyCorrect: An anal fistula is a tract connecting the anal canal to the perianal skin and represents the chronic form of cryptoglandular infection. After an abscess drains, failure of the internal opening to close leaves a persistent tract, and patients present with persistent or recurrent perianal drainage from a small opening near the anus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An anal fissure is a tear in the anoderm causing sharp pain with defecation and bright red blood, not continuous purulent drainage from a skin opening.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pruritus ani is intense perianal itching; drainage from a discrete external opening is not its defining feature.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A recurrent abscess would produce constant throbbing pain with a tender, fluctuant, erythematous swelling, which is explicitly absent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A thrombosed external hemorrhoid is an acutely painful bluish lump at the anal verge and does not drain pus chronically.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Correct: a chronic tract with persistent drainage from a small opening near the anus after an abscess is fistula-in-ano.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman is about to undergo incision and drainage of a perianal abscess. She asks what problem she is most likely to encounter after the procedure. Which of the following complications should she be counseled about as the most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Development of a chronic posterior midline anal fissure

choices.label: B
choices.text: Prolapse of internal hemorrhoids requiring manual reduction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fecal incontinence

choices.label: D
choices.text: A chronic tract with recurrent perianal drainage

choices.label: E
choices.text: Anal squamous cell carcinoma

explanation.summary: Fistula formation is the expected sequela after drainage of a perianal abscess.
explanation.whyCorrect: After an anal abscess drains externally, either spontaneously or by incision, failure of the internal opening to close may leave a persistent tract between the anal canal and the skin. This occurs in 30% to 50% of patients and presents as persistent or recurrent perianal drainage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anal fissures result from a tear of the anoderm caused by hard stool, not from drainage of an abscess.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Internal hemorrhoidal prolapse results from degradation of the supporting connective tissue with straining and is unrelated to abscess drainage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fecal incontinence is a concern with operations that divide sphincter muscle, such as fistulotomy for a complex fistula or sphincterotomy, not with simple abscess drainage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Correct: 30% to 50% of patients develop a persistent tract, a fistula-in-ano, with recurrent perianal drainage after an abscess drains.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anal squamous cell carcinoma is driven by persistent HPV infection and is not a consequence of abscess drainage.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has 4 days of severe rectal pain and fever to 38.6 C (101.5 F). The perianal skin appears normal, with no swelling, erythema, or fluctuance. Digital examination elicits severe pain and reveals focal firmness along the right wall of the anal canal, but the examination cannot be completed because of pain. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reassurance with fiber supplementation and follow-up in 6 weeks

choices.label: B
choices.text: Topical nitroglycerin ointment

choices.label: C
choices.text: Examination under anesthesia with drainage of the collection

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral antibiotics alone with outpatient follow-up

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rubber band ligation

explanation.summary: A deep anorectal abscess without external findings requires examination under anesthesia and drainage.
explanation.whyCorrect: Deeper abscesses (intersphincteric and ischiorectal) may present with rectal pain, fever, and focal firmness without obvious external findings, and may require examination under anesthesia. Abscesses in deep or tight anatomic spaces feel indurated or focally firm rather than fluctuant, and the treatment remains prompt drainage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fiber and observation address constipation and fissure prevention and would allow an undrained deep abscess to make the patient increasingly ill.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Topical nitroglycerin targets internal sphincter spasm in anal fissures and has no role in an undrained abscess.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Correct: a febrile patient with rectal pain and focal firmness but no external findings likely has a deep abscess requiring examination under anesthesia and drainage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antibiotics are an adjunct at most and do not achieve source control; drainage is required.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rubber band ligation treats symptomatic internal hemorrhoids and would not address an abscess.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman is diagnosed with an anal fissure after passing a hard stool. Disruption of which of the following structures accounts for her lesion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The anoderm distal to the dentate line

choices.label: B
choices.text: The columnar mucosa above the dentate line

choices.label: C
choices.text: The internal anal sphincter muscle

choices.label: D
choices.text: The puborectalis component of the levator ani

choices.label: E
choices.text: The epithelial lining of an anal crypt gland

explanation.summary: Tests the anatomic definition of an anal fissure.
explanation.whyCorrect: An anal fissure is a tear in the anoderm, the squamous epithelium below the dentate line. Because the anoderm has somatic innervation, the tear produces sharp, tearing pain during defecation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Correct: a fissure is a tear in the anoderm, the squamous epithelium below the dentate line.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The columnar mucosa above the dentate line is viscerally innervated and is the covering of internal hemorrhoids, which bleed painlessly; a tear there would not cause sharp pain.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Internal sphincter fibers may become visible at the base of a chronic fissure, but the injury itself is of the overlying anoderm; the muscle is affected by reflex spasm, not by the initial tear.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The puborectalis is a pelvic floor muscle at the anorectal junction and is not disrupted by passage of a hard stool.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Obstruction and infection of an anal crypt gland produces a perianal abscess or fistula, not a fissure.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man has had pain with defecation and a few drops of bright red blood for 8 days after a bout of constipation. Examination shows a simple tear in the posterior midline anoderm without a skin tag or exposed muscle fibers. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lateral internal sphincterotomy under general anesthesia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fistulotomy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rubber band ligation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Incision and drainage of the perianal space

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fiber, stool softeners, and sitz baths

explanation.summary: Acute anal fissures are managed conservatively first.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute fissures typically heal with fiber supplementation, stool softeners, and sitz baths. The simple tear without a sentinel tag or exposed sphincter fibers identifies this as an acute rather than chronic fissure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lateral internal sphincterotomy is reserved for chronic fissures refractory to medical therapy, not for an 8-day-old acute fissure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fistulotomy lays open a simple, low fistula tract; there is no fistula here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rubber band ligation treats symptomatic internal hemorrhoids above the dentate line and would not address an anoderm tear.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Incision and drainage treats a perianal abscess; there is no fluid collection in this patient.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Correct: acute fissures typically heal with fiber, stool softeners, and sitz baths.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man has had a posterior midline anal fissure for 5 months, with a sentinel skin tag and visible sphincter fibers at the ulcer base. He has completed prolonged trials of fiber, stool softeners, sitz baths, topical nifedipine, and topical nitroglycerin without healing. He has normal continence. Which of the following is the most effective next treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Another 8-week course of the same topical therapy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lateral internal sphincterotomy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fistulotomy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hemorrhoidectomy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Excision of the sentinel skin tag alone

explanation.summary: Lateral internal sphincterotomy is the definitive treatment for a refractory chronic fissure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lateral internal sphincterotomy permanently reduces excessive resting internal anal sphincter tone and is the most effective treatment for chronic anal fissures refractory to medical therapy, with excellent healing rates. This patient has failed adequate medical therapy and has normal baseline continence.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Repeating therapy that has already failed over months is unlikely to heal a chronic fissure with established chronic features.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Correct: lateral internal sphincterotomy permanently lowers resting internal sphincter tone and is the most effective treatment for medically refractory chronic fissures.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fistulotomy lays open a fistula tract and does not treat a fissure or the underlying sphincter hypertonicity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemorrhoidectomy is for grade III-IV or mixed hemorrhoidal disease refractory to less invasive treatment, not for a fissure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Removing the sentinel tag does not address the internal sphincter spasm and ischemia that prevent fissure healing.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman with a chronic posterior midline anal fissure that has not healed with fiber, sitz baths, and topical calcium channel blocker therapy is being considered for lateral internal sphincterotomy. Which of the following elements of her history is most important to elicit before offering this operation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Prior treatment for internal hemorrhoids

choices.label: B
choices.text: Daily dietary fiber intake

choices.label: C
choices.text: History of receptive anal intercourse

choices.label: D
choices.text: Baseline fecal incontinence

choices.label: E
choices.text: Family history of colorectal cancer

explanation.summary: Tests the key patient-selection caveat for lateral internal sphincterotomy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lateral internal sphincterotomy permanently reduces resting internal sphincter tone. Most patients tolerate this reduction in sphincter hypertonicity well, but the procedure may not be ideal for patients with baseline fecal incontinence, so preexisting continence must be assessed first.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Prior hemorrhoid treatment does not change the risk or suitability of dividing the internal sphincter for a fissure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fiber intake matters for stool consistency and initial fissure management, but it is not the determining factor in whether sphincterotomy is safe.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Receptive anal intercourse is relevant to infectious proctitis, not to the continence risk of sphincterotomy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Correct: sphincterotomy permanently lowers sphincter tone and may not be ideal for a patient with baseline fecal incontinence.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A family history of colorectal cancer guides colonoscopy decisions and does not affect the safety of sphincterotomy.

questions.stem: A medical student is asked to describe the anatomy of the structures whose obstruction gives rise to perianal abscesses and fistulas. Which of the following best describes these structures?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They open onto the rectal mucosa above the transverse rectal folds of Houston

choices.label: B
choices.text: They drain directly into the external hemorrhoidal plexus

choices.label: C
choices.text: They drain into dentate-line crypts and the intersphincteric space

choices.label: D
choices.text: They lie within the iliococcygeus portion of the levator ani muscle

choices.label: E
choices.text: They open onto the perianal skin at the anal verge

explanation.summary: Tests the anatomy of the anal glands, the source of cryptoglandular infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: The anal glands open into crypts at the dentate line and extend into the intersphincteric space. Obstruction of these glands is the origin of perianal abscesses and fistulas, and their intersphincteric course explains how infection reaches the perianal, intersphincteric, and ischiorectal spaces.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The anal glands open at the dentate line in the anal canal, not into the rectum proximal to the valves of Houston.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The anal glands are secretory structures draining into anal crypts; they are not tributaries of the external hemorrhoidal venous plexus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Correct: the anal glands open into crypts at the dentate line and extend into the intersphincteric space, and their obstruction causes abscesses and fistulas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The levator ani is skeletal pelvic floor muscle at the anorectal junction and does not contain the anal glands.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An opening on the perianal skin describes the external opening of an established fistula, not the normal anatomy of the anal glands.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man has 5 days of deep, throbbing pain in the buttock and rectum with a temperature of 38.7 C (101.7 F). There is no discrete fluctuant lump at the anal verge, but the tissue lateral to the sphincter complex is diffusely indurated, warm, and exquisitely tender, and digital examination shows firmness in the fat lateral to the anal canal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ischiorectal abscess

choices.label: B
choices.text: Perianal abscess

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intersphincteric abscess

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fistula-in-ano

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrombosed external hemorrhoid

explanation.summary: Tests classification of anorectal abscesses by anatomic space.
explanation.whyCorrect: The ischiorectal (ischioanal) abscess occupies the fat lateral to the sphincter complex, which matches the diffuse induration and firmness lateral to the anal canal. As a deeper abscess it presents with rectal pain, fever, and focal firmness rather than an obvious superficial fluctuant lump.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Correct: a febrile patient with induration and firmness in the fat lateral to the sphincter complex has an ischiorectal (ischioanal) abscess.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A perianal abscess is the most common type but is superficial at the anal verge and is typically visible and palpable as a discrete fluctuant swelling, which is absent here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An intersphincteric abscess lies between the internal and external sphincters and would not produce induration of the fat lateral to the sphincter complex.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fistula-in-ano is a chronic tract causing persistent drainage from a small skin opening rather than an acute febrile inflammatory mass.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A thrombosed external hemorrhoid is a firm bluish lump at the anal verge without fever or deep induration.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman has had a posterior midline anal fissure for 3 months despite stool softeners. Which of the following best explains why her fissure has failed to heal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Thrombosis of the internal hemorrhoidal plexus causing mucosal infarction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bacterial superinfection of obstructed anal glands at the base of the tear

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of somatic innervation of the anoderm impairing wound signaling

choices.label: D
choices.text: Chronic stretch injury of the pudendal nerve from straining

choices.label: E
choices.text: Internal sphincter spasm that reduces posterior midline perfusion

explanation.summary: Tests the pain-spasm-ischemia cycle that produces chronic anal fissures.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fissure pain triggers reflex internal sphincter spasm and hypertrophy. This spasm reduces blood flow to the posterior midline, which already has the poorest blood supply in the anal canal, impairing healing and creating the cycle of pain, spasm, ischemia, and non-healing.
